a: Cognitive Load Theory is used to manage the mental effort required during complex learning by addressing intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive loads. This framework helps ensure students can manage tasks effectively and focus on demonstrating required competencies.

q: What methodology was used to develop the multimedia courseware?
a: The study employed a multi-stage qualitative and developmental approach involving key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and roundtable discussions with content experts, instructional designers, and multimedia specialists. A pilot review with ten students was also conducted to evaluate the content, activities, and design.

q: What were the results of the pilot review conducted with students?
a: Students provided positive responses regarding the relevance, presentation, and multimedia mix of the courseware. However, they suggested improvements for navigation and the addition of a tutorial guide.

q: Who benefits most from the application of this research?
a: Nursing students benefit by having opportunities to maximize their learning potentials during clinical practicum through new learning methods and computer-assisted learning. The multimedia courseware helps them manage tasks more effectively, reduce time spent on unnecessary steps, and focus on learning and demonstrating required competencies.

q: How does the research influence the way tasks are selected for course design?
a: The development of multimedia courseware using Cognitive Load Theory involves selecting tasks needed by nurses in the clinical practicum. This process includes simplifying the complexity of tasks, reducing extraneous cognitive load, and refocusing learners to the subject matter.

q: What role do self-assessment questions play in the design of this courseware?
a: Self-assessment questions help in formative evaluation and were available in both interactive and offline formats.

q: How does the multimedia environment mimic a real-world setting for distance learners?
a: The multimedia environment was kept similar to the real setting through the structure of the hospital unit, the arrangement of rooms, and the look-and-feel of the nurses’ station and patient rooms.

q: What feedback did students provide regarding the technology's usability?
a: Students rated the courseware as very good in terms of presentation, relevance, level of interest generated, clarity, readability, appropriateness, and good mix of multimedia elements and design. There were some comments on how to improve navigation of the course, and some students requested a basic tutorial guide on the features of the courseware.

q: How does addressing extraneous load benefit the student?
a: Reducing extraneous load helps students reduce the time spent on unnecessary steps when trying to understand concepts. This allows them to focus more effectively on learning and demonstrating required competencies.

q: What specific multimedia elements were used to reduce cognitive overload?
a: The case studies were rendered in video formats that were “chunked” into short video clips corresponding to each identified task and sub-task. These short videos were made realistic by being taken in the vernacular language with English subtitles.

q: Why is a virtual practicum necessary for distance learning nursing students?
a: A virtual practicum helps bridge the gap between theory and practice when students lack access to physical preceptors. It provides a way to master complex clinical skills in a distance-learning environment.

q: What are the primary advantages of distance education for nursing students?
a: Distance education offers the convenience of pursuing formal education without leaving jobs or being separated from families. It also provides opportunities for the immediate application of learning to work and allows for savings in time and money.

q: What specific challenges does distance education pose for the nursing discipline?
a: Distance education faces challenges because nursing skills and personal qualities are traditionally learned through face-to-face interaction. Additionally, there is a need to provide continuous interaction to replace the intellectual discourse found in physical classrooms.

q: What are the identified needs for nursing students enrolled in distance education programs?
a: Students require instruction on new learning methods, computer-assisted learning, and educational technology. There is also a documented need to provide for the development of a professional technical language.

q: How can an instructor manage intrinsic cognitive load?
a: While intrinsic cognitive load cannot be altered by the instructor, it can be broken into individual subschemas. These subschemas can be taught in isolation before being brought back together as a combined whole.

q: What is the primary purpose of the research conducted by Calora and Lleva?
a: The research aims to evaluate the use and acceptance of eLearning technologies among senior high school students in a private high school in Los Baños, Laguna. It specifically seeks to determine students' preconceived notions about eLearning and their behavioral intention to pursue tertiary education online.

q: What were the main findings regarding students' intention to pursue online tertiary education?
a: The majority of respondents had a positive behavioral intention to pursue tertiary education through eLearning, meaning they were willing to take tertiary education online. Of the UTAUT constructs, only performance expectancy was found to be a significant predictor of this behavioral intention.

q: Which UTAUT2 construct was identified as the only significant predictor of behavioral intention?
a: Performance expectancy was the only construct found to be a significant predictor of behavioral intention. This means students were more likely to intend to pursue online education if they believed eLearning would help them achieve their academic goals.

q: What specific knowledge gaps were identified among the senior high school students surveyed?
a: Only 38.5% of respondents had knowledge about technologies that enabled students to take exams or submit assignments online. Additionally, only 18% believed collaboration between students was possible.

q: What are the key recommendations for educational institutions based on these findings?
a: Institutions are encouraged to implement detailed information, education, and communication (IEC) campaigns to explain online system functions. Additionally, developers should prioritize resource accessibility, student support, interactive environments, and visible teacher presence.

q: Who is the primary target audience for the findings of this research?
a: The findings will enable educators to design online curricula or programs that cater to the needs of potential students. They will also help eLearning institutions in the process of promoting their courses to the possible influx of higher education students.

q: What device do students primarily use to access learning technologies?
a: Most participants in the study primarily use smartphones to access the internet for their technology-related activities.

q: Why are eLearning and Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) considered important in the Philippine context?
a: eLearning technologies can address the inadequacy of current infrastructure and maximize existing technologies to address teaching and learning gaps. Its primary purpose is to increase accessibility of education and reduce transportation and infrastructure costs, while ODeL presents a solution to the residential limits of traditional universities.

q: What are the recommended features for developers of eLearning technologies?
a: Developers should prioritize resource accessibility, student support, and the creation of engaging, interactive, and collaborative environments. They should also focus on ensuring a visible teacher presence to encourage student success.

q: What communication strategy is recommended to help students navigate eLearning technologies?
a: Institutions should implement detailed information, education, and communication (IEC) campaigns. These campaigns should explain how online learning systems function and how they can help students meet their academic goals.

q: How did social influence relate to the sex of the respondents?
a: A weak association was observed between sex and social influence. Additionally, male respondents were more likely to have significant others who had a positive impression of eLearning technologies.

q: How was the UTAUT2 framework applied in this research?
a: The researchers used the UTAUT2 framework to examine the moderating effects of various constructs on the behavioral intention of 200 senior high school students. This was done through the use of correlation and regression analysis.

q: What challenges does the Philippine educational system face according to the Philippine Development Plan 2017-2022?
a: Most challenges in educational reform initiatives are caused by a lack of human capital development. There is a significant need to improve educational services and facilities to increase student participation rates.

q: Why do traditional residential universities face problems due to the 2018 K to 12 Program graduates?
a: The first batch of graduates created a surplus of potential college students. This influx poses problems for traditional universities because they lack the human, financial, and physical resources to accommodate them.

q: What are the specific definitions of PE and EE within the UTAUT framework used in this research?
a: Performance Expectancy (PE) is the degree to which respondents believe using eLearning technologies helps achieve academic goals. Effort Expectancy (EE) refers to the respondents' belief regarding the amount of effort required to use these technologies.

q: What are the emerging roles for teachers in technology-mediated environments?
a: The new teacher roles are in the areas of instructional design, training, collaborative partner in learning, and team coordinating. Additionally, teachers may transition from being information transmitters to guides who arrange meaningful learner-centred experiences.

q: What research methodology was used to reach these conclusions?
a: The study employed a review-based research approach by synthesizing findings from 50 research papers. Additionally, primary data was gathered through informal interactions with teachers at various state and national open universities.

q: How has the evolution of distance education changed the learner profile?
a: The shift from postal services to digital tools like blogs and social media has created students who seek flexibility and real-time collaboration. These learners now have instant access to vast online resources, changing how they interact with instructors.

q: What are the main barriers to implementing technology in distance education?
a: Implementation is hindered by a lack of monetary resources, insufficient staff training, and a lack of expertise in course design. Administrative and legal constraints can also limit the use of emerging technologies.

q: What are the implications for educational institutions regarding professional development?
a: Professional development is needed to update distance education teachers regarding the use of technology in distance education. Additionally, teachers should be allowed to choose, willing to make choices, and qualified to implement their choices effectively.

q: How does technology impact the traditional authority of the teacher?
a: With increased access to resources on the Web, the teacher is no longer the "dispenser of information." As teaching becomes more learner-centered, faculty fear that their role will be replaced by technology and they will ultimately lose their authority over the classrooms.

q: What is the 'transactional distance gap' in the context of this research?
a: The transactional distance gap refers to the communication gap caused by geographic separation. To overcome this, teachers must be empowered to act as guides and collaborators to foster meaningful interaction.

q: What psychological challenges do teachers face during this technological transition?
a: Faculty fear that their role will be replaced by technology and that they will lose their authority over classrooms. They also experience anxiety regarding job security, changes within the field, and concerns that online programs will replace on-campus learning experiences.

q: What is a major obstacle to effective course design in distance education?
a: A significant challenge is the lack of expertise in course design and delivery. This is often compounded by a lack of monetary resources and insufficient staff training.

q: How has the medium of distance education changed over time?
a: Distance education has evolved from traditional postal services and physical media to digital tools like e-mail, blogs, wikis, and social media. This evolution has transformed the teaching and learning processes.

q: How does the role of the teacher change when students have instant access to online resources?
a: With increased access to resources on the Web, the teacher is no longer the "dispenser of information." Students are no longer dependent on the teacher alone for knowledge, and the instructor's role changes from an information transmitter to a guide who arranges meaningful learner-centred experiences.

q: What new roles do teachers adopt to facilitate knowledge exchange?
a: New teacher roles include being a team coordinator, instructional designer, trainer, and collaborative partner in learning. Additionally, in distance education, teachers may act as scriptwriters, audio and video production specialists, programmers, multimedia course authors, and web-developers.

q: What characterizes the modern learner in distance education?
a: Modern learners seek flexibility and real-time collaboration. They are often digitally native and have instant access to vast online resources.

q: What is required to ensure the success of technology-mediated distance education?
a: Effective faculty participation is the key driving factor towards the success of technology-mediated distance education.

q: How has the delivery of distance education materials evolved over time?
a: Distance learning previously relied on sending study materials and receiving assignments via post. This evolved to using e-mail and digital repositories, and eventually integrated social media tools, blogs, wikis, and discussion forums.

q: What is the primary objective of the research conducted by Ramos and Ballera?
a: The research aims to analyze electroencephalogram (EEG) signals to determine attention, emotion, and cognitive load as factors for recommending appropriate learning pedagogies. The goal is to develop a rule-based pedagogy for individual learners.

q: What methodology and tools were used to collect and process the brain signal data?
a: The Emotiv EPOC+14 Channel Mobile Encephalogram (EEG) tool was used to record data, which was then processed using the MATLAB EEG tool. Processing methods included Bandpass and infinite impulse response (IIR) filters for noise removal, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for feature extraction, discrete wavelet transforms, and Independent Component Analysis (ICA) with a runica method. Additionally, the autocorrelation function and Welch's Periodogram method were used to estimate the power spectrum and compute Fourier transforms.

q: How were the different mental load components combined for the analysis?
a: The final values for attention load, emotion load, and cognitive load were aggregated using weighted means. These aggregated values were then used as independent variables in a regression model to predict performance scores.

q: What were the main findings regarding the relationship between mental loads and the learning process?
a: The simulation demonstrated that the combined values of attention, emotion, and cognition are significant predictors of the learning process. The study established a mapping system using expert judgment to prioritize pedagogies based on signal classification.

q: What are the key recommendations for implementing this research in e-learning systems?
a: The authors recommend an individualized rule-based pedagogy that incorporates EEG instruments to collect affective and cognitive attributes. This approach allows learners to adjust to their learning process with minimal supervision from educational strategists.

q: What are the broader implications of integrating EEG technology into digital education?
a: Using an EEG tool for diagnostic assessment of a learner's mental state could enable real-time assessments in e-learning and generate data for stakeholders' decision-making. Additionally, incorporating the EEG instrument to collect affective and cognitive attributes could help learners adjust better and follow their learning process with minimal supervision.

q: What was the specific participant demographic used in the experimental design?
a: The study involved 20 respondents, consisting of 10 males and 10 females, all of whom had a background in C++ programming.

q: What role does data-driven assessment play in the proposed pedagogical framework?
a: Data-driven assessment, including the analysis of EEG signals for attention, emotion, and cognition, serves as a basis for stakeholders' decision-making and helps determine which component most substantially influences the learning process. These assessments allow for the implementation of more appropriate, individualized rule-based pedagogies and help improve teaching-learning outcomes.

q: What factors contribute to negative learner experiences in virtual learning environments?
a: Negative learner experiences are influenced by complex learning content presentations, visual displays, and faulty learning materials that cause confusion. Additionally, learners experience anxiety and frustration due to task irrelevancy, excessive boredom, and extremely difficult learning tasks that distribute cognitive load.

q: How can the proposed rule-based pedagogy improve the learner's experience?
a: The individualized rule-based pedagogy incorporates the EEG instrument to collect affective and cognitive attributes, which can help learners adjust better and follow their learning process with minimal supervision. Additionally, it provides information to educational strategists to improve learning materials by investigating the attention and emotion of learners and the cognitive load.

q: How can implementing this research benefit current e-learning systems?
a: Implementing this study would provide tremendous learning benefits and improvements in the teaching-learning process. It allows for more effective monitoring of learner status to improve overall outcomes.

q: What specific tool was used to record the electroencephalogram signals in this research?
a: The Emotiv EPOC+14 Channel Mobile Encephalogram (EEG) tool recorded the learners' attention, cognition, and emotion every 20 seconds.

q: How were the electroencephalogram signals processed to ensure data quality?
a: The signals were processed using MATLAB EEG tools and various algorithms like Bandpass filters, IIR filters, PCA, and ICA. These methods were applied to process the signals and remove noise from the data.

q: What was the purpose of aggregating the attention, emotion, and cognition loads?
a: The values were aggregated to serve as inputs for a regression model to predict learners' performance scores. This aggregation helps in creating a cohesive pedagogical framework from individual components.

q: What specific characteristics define a learner's attention?
a: Attention includes the individual capacity for information processing, attentiveness, inattention, divided attention, flexibility, and sustained attention. It also varies according to individual preferences and circumstances.

q: What criteria were used to select the respondents for the purposive sampling technique?
a: Respondents were selected based on having a Master's or Doctoral degree in education. Additionally, they were required to have at least five years of teaching experience.

q: What is the primary purpose of the research conducted by Ridulme and Sales?
a: The research aims to identify the challenges and learning experiences of first-year graduate nursing students in an open and distance education program. The findings are intended to help construct new strategies and practices for future program development.

q: What were the main findings regarding the experiences of graduate nursing students in open and distance learning?
a: The biggest challenge faced by participants was disciplining themselves to stick to their time management plan. The best experience was being able to study at their own pace and at their workplace, while the least liked experience was the delayed responses of professors to important queries.

q: What research methodology was used to investigate these student experiences?
a: The researchers employed a qualitative research design guided by Gibbs’ Reflective Cycle. Data was collected from 13 graduate nursing students through an online self-administered questionnaire.

q: What are the key recommendations for instructors to improve the graduate nursing program?
a: Instructors should give feedback to students using different online methods such as e-mail, student portal, or polls. Additionally, they should follow guidelines for responses and provide feedback in the form of questions, suggestions, and statements to help students improve their work.

q: Who will benefit most from the implementation of the proposed program improvements?
a: The new strategies and practices constructed from the students' reflections are intended for the development of the program for future students.

q: What were the most significant grievances reported by the graduate nursing students?
a: The biggest challenge participants faced was disciplining themselves to stick to their time management plan. Additionally, the least liked experience was the delayed responses of professors to important queries, which sometimes took a week or a month.

q: What were the primary technical barriers encountered by students in the distance learning environment?
a: Technical barriers included poor internet connection, online interruptions, technical problems, password confusion, and power interruptions. Additionally, some students lacked the hardware or software capability to receive videos and other materials via the web.

q: What is the main internal struggle students faced regarding their academic responsibilities?
a: The biggest hurdle for students was the self-discipline required for effective time management. They found it difficult to balance work, social life, and academic responsibilities when assignments had overlapping deadlines.

q: What are the limitations of the scope of this research?
a: The study focused specifically on first-year graduate nursing students in an open university in the Philippines. The authors suggest that future research should expand these investigations to undergraduate programs.

q: How did the flexibility of distance learning impact the student experience?
a: Being able to study at their own pace and at their workplace taught students to be more responsible and independent. Additionally, distance learners have greater freedom to choose how to learn and have opportunities to shape their learning to be relevant to who they are and where they are at any given time.

q: What specific support mechanisms were identified as beneficial for students?
a: Students noted that support from both professors and peers was a significant motivator. This social and academic support helped balance the challenges of the distance learning mode.

q: How were student reflections used as a research tool?
a: The researchers used written reflections from students' first year to identify specific challenges and learning experiences. These reflections provided qualitative data to help construct new program development strategies.

q: What were the primary external barriers to student success in the program?
a: The primary external barriers included poor internet connection, online interruptions, technical problems, and password confusion. Additionally, students faced power interruptions, weak online signals, and lack of hardware or software capability to receive digital materials.

q: What are the primary advantages of open and distance learning?
a: Open and distance learning offers wider access and cost-efficiency for students. Additionally, advancements in information and communication technologies provide new opportunities for sharing resources and networking with peers and instructors.

q: What is the primary problem addressed by the researchers regarding bioinformatics education?
a: The most challenging task is selecting compatible software tools to include in open and distance learning (ODL) courses. Additionally, there are no recorded criteria to evaluate these bioinformatics software tools for their compatibility for ODL.

q: What methodology did the researchers use to evaluate the bioinformatics tools?
a: The researchers employed a criteria-based software evaluation method using two main categories: Usability and Maintainability. Each criterion was scored as either 1 (compliant) or 0 (non-compliant) to determine a tool's total user-friendliness percentage.

q: What were the key findings regarding the usability of the evaluated bioinformatics tools?
a: The findings showed that while most tools clearly state their primary functions, only 60% provide comprehensive manuals and only 15% offer audio-visual tutorials. There is also a notable gap in peer-assisted resources, with only 42% of tools including an FAQ section.

q: Who benefits from the implementation of these findings?
a: The outcome facilitates offering hard science concepts with minimum commitment of resources and time to meet the escalating demand for capacity development in Bioinformatics. Additionally, the flexibility of ODL facilitates those who missed the opportunity to learn Bioinformatics in secondary and undergraduate education or mid-career developers needing to develop their knowledge and skills.

q: How does the reliance on information and communication technology (ICT) impact the delivery of bioinformatics?
a: Bioinformatics can be easily offered in open and distance (e)learning (ODL/ODeL) systems due to its total reliance on information and computer technology (ICT). Unlike most life science subjects, bioinformatics requires limited physical resources, such as access to a computer and the Internet.

q: How can existing bioinformatics software help in the process of course design?
a: Using existing bioinformatics software tools and allied documentation can drastically reduce the time and resources required for designing and updating courses. This helps educators manage the rapid evolution of the field.

q: What specific type of bioinformatics analysis was a focus of the evaluation?
a: The researchers paid particular attention to tools specialized for plant genomic analysis. The evaluation covered a wide spectrum of tools, from simple sequence analysis to genome-wide analysis.

q: Why is bioinformatics considered well-suited for Open and Distance Learning (ODL)?
a: Bioinformatics can be easily offered in ODL systems due to its total reliance on information and computer technology (ICT). Unlike most life science subjects, it requires limited physical resources such as access to a computer and the Internet.

q: What are the primary challenges in developing bioinformatics curricula within ODL systems?
a: The introduction of ODL courses demands considerable resources and time for course design, content development, and delivery. The most challenging task is selecting compatible software tools, as there are no recorded criteria to evaluate these tools for ODL compatibility. Additionally, identifying user-friendly tools requires multidisciplinary knowledge in ODL, Biology, and Bioinformatics.

q: How can ODeL institutions meet the growing demand for bioinformatics professionals?
a: Institutions can meet demand efficiently by integrating high-quality, existing software and open learning resources. This strategy minimizes the commitment of resources and time required for capacity development.

q: Which scientific disciplines contribute to the field of bioinformatics?
a: Bioinformatics merges biology and computer sciences. It also requires substantial inputs from mathematics, statistics, information technology, physics, and chemistry.

q: What are the primary components of bioinformatics infrastructure?
a: The infrastructure consists of publicly available databases, software tools for data analysis, and integrated bioinformatics platforms (IBP). These databases are specialized based on the type of data they curate, such as DNA or protein sequence.

q: Which integrated bioinformatics platforms are noted for providing excellent teaching and learning material?
a: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) and the European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) are the most versatile platforms. They integrate various software tools to mine data ranging from literature to genomic and proteomic information.

q: How can bioinformatics software tools assist in the development of ODL courses?
a: Including bioinformatics software tools and allied documentation in course contents can significantly reduce the time and resources spent on course development. This inclusion also makes courses more amenable to the rapid changes occurring in the bioinformatics field.

q: What specific criteria were used to evaluate the bioinformatics software tools in this analysis?
a: The analysis primarily used usability and maintainability guidelines adopted from the Software Evaluation Criteria by Jackson, Crouch, and Baxter. A scoring system was applied where a score of 1 was given for compliance and 0 for non-compliance.

q: What is the central purpose of investigating teaching presence in the Philippine K-12 Alternative Delivery Mode?
a: This exploratory case study sought to capture the interactions and experiences in three blended learning classes through the elements of the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework. It aimed to investigate teacher and student blended learning interactions.

q: What are the main findings regarding how teaching presence is manifested in K-12 blended learning classes?
a: Teaching presence is strongly manifested through teacher roles in design, organization, and discourse facilitation, which helps build learning communities. Additionally, students exhibit teaching-like behaviors through peer-facilitation and self-regulation during collaborative tasks.

q: What research method and approach were used to examine these blended learning interactions?
a: The researcher employed an exploratory case study design involving three blended learning classes from urban public schools. Data was gathered through interviews, focus group discussions, classroom observations, field notes, and data from Learning Management Systems and Facebook Messenger.

q: Who can benefit from the implementation of the proposed CoI Self-Reflection Tool for Teachers?
a: The tool is proposed for inclusion in teacher preparation endeavors for BL in schools and for use in school-based professional development of teachers. It can also be used in in-service teacher training activities for self and collaborative reflection on remote, blended, or fully online class teaching experiences.

q: What role does student behavior play in the manifestation of teaching presence in this context?
a: Students manifest teaching presence through directing and regulating their own learning. They also engage in peer-facilitation, where they teach classmates who are struggling to understand content during collaborative tasks.

q: What limitations or challenges were noted regarding teacher presence in digital environments?
a: Some students perceived teachers as less present online because they did not seem proficient with technology or were not trained in using the LMS and other educational applications. Additionally, miscommunications occurred because students sometimes had difficulty accessing platforms due to bugs and updates.

q: How does technological proficiency affect the perception of teacher presence in K-12 blended learning?
a: Grade 10 students sensed that not all teachers seem to be proficient with technology and thus were perceived as less present when online. Some students noted that some teachers did not seem to be trained in the use of the LMS or know how to use other applications for educational purposes.

q: What challenges did students face regarding feedback and communication in blended learning?
a: Areas for improvement related to teaching presence were revealed, particularly in communication, the timeliness of feedback, and the online facilitation of discourse. The timeliness of feedback received the lowest mean rating among survey items, suggesting it may be an area of concern for some students.

q: How do students demonstrate self-regulation during collaborative tasks?
a: Students exhibit teaching-like behaviors through peer-facilitation to help struggling classmates. They also manifest teaching presence by directing and regulating their own learning processes.

q: Is teaching presence limited only to the instructor in K-12 blended learning settings?
a: No, the study revealed that teaching presence is not exclusive to instructors. Students also manifest teaching-like behaviors through peer support and regulatory roles.

q: How does the Community of Inquiry framework assist in understanding K-12 blended learning?
a: The CoI framework serves as a practical tool to understand and guide teaching and learning in K-12 blended learning programs. It emphasizes the interplay of social, cognitive, and teaching presence.

q: What modification is suggested for the Community of Inquiry framework to better suit K-12 students?
a: Changes to the categories and indicators of the CoI are suggested, including the proposal of an additional category for the element of TP called Self-direction with indicators of monitoring/knowledge of cognition and strategy use. Additionally, it is suggested that items from the Shared Metacognition Questionnaire of Garrison and Akyol (2015) be accommodated within the CoI survey instrument for use among K-12 students.

q: What is the purpose of the Alternative Delivery Mode in the Philippine K-12 system?
a: The Alternative Delivery Mode aims to reduce dropout rates and provide educational access to students in unusual circumstances. Blended learning is a core component of these programs.

q: How did teachers facilitate discourse in the K-12 blended learning classes studied?
a: To guide student discussion when online, the English teacher posted polls and questions on controversial issues or current events. Teachers and students alike have been found to facilitate discourse by prompting student contributions.

q: What are the three elements of the Community of Inquiry framework?
a: The three elements are teaching presence (TP), cognitive presence (CP), and social presence (SP). These elements must interplay to create a fruitful online community of learning.

q: What specific survey item regarding feedback received the lowest mean rating?
a: Item TP13, which pertains to the timeliness of feedback, received the lowest mean rating of 3.57. This suggests that the timeliness of feedback may be a concern for some students.

q: In what setting is facilitating discourse most frequently demonstrated by teachers?
a: Facilitating discourse is most frequently demonstrated during face-to-face sessions, with a coding count of 35 compared to two for online classes. This category includes setting the climate for learning, prompting discussion, and reinforcing student contributions.

q: What was a notable observation regarding the framing of the CoI Survey items?
a: Most items under teaching presence were framed from the student's point of view regarding the teacher's actions rather than the students' roles. Specifically, 12 out of 13 items began with the word "The teacher."

q: What is the primary purpose of exploring ticketing-based student support systems in Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environments?
a: The research investigates how automated ticketing systems can enhance quality assurance in student support services within ODeL settings. These systems aim to provide reliable and timely support to facilitate student retention and success where face-to-face interaction is limited.

q: What are the main findings regarding the benefits of implementing a ticketing-based system?
a: Ticketing-based systems offer improved workflows through automation, 24/7 access to a knowledge base, and data analytics insights. The implementation of Freshdesk specifically provided a centralized knowledge base that allows students to find accurate, up-to-date solutions via articles.

q: What are the key recommendations for ODeL institutions considering these systems?
a: The university should keep students' needs in mind when implementing technology-based support systems, taking into account ease of use and complexity. There should be more activities to inform students about proper support channels, and services should cater to a wide range of students by considering different learning styles. Additionally, support staff should receive adequate training before implementing any student support system.

q: Who are the primary stakeholders affected by these student support changes?
a: The primary stakeholders include ODeL students, support staff, and faculty members. The study specifically looked at the experiences of BAMS students, alumni, and staff at the University of the Philippines Open University.

q: What are the implications of adopting a ticketing-based system for university quality assurance?
a: A ticketing-based system can serve as part of an ODeL institution’s quality assurance initiatives in student support. It keeps the support process efficient and responsive while allowing universities to identify areas for improvement through automation, reporting, macros, and tracking features.

q: What is the definition of a ticketing-based system in the context of this research?
a: A ticketing-based system is an automated tool used to track queries until resolution and provide a centralized knowledge base. It serves as a quality assurance intervention to make student support processes more efficient and responsive.

q: How does information fragmentation affect student access to support at UPOU?
a: Students previously relied on at least eight different formal and informal online sources for information. This fragmentation leads to confusion and the risk of students following outdated or conflicting information.

q: How can a ticketing-based system improve the accessibility of information for ODeL students?
a: The system provides 24/7 access to a knowledge base where students can find solutions via articles. This allows students to find information independently before needing to file a formal ticket.

q: How does student support relate to quality assurance in higher education?
a: Effective student support is considered one of the most important dimensions of quality assurance in higher education. In ODeL settings, reliable support is vital for student retention and success.

q: What institutional challenges regarding policy and records were identified?
a: Institutions faced difficulties with record-keeping, document tracking, and maintaining information during staff turnover. There were also challenges in providing clearly defined academic and administrative policies.

q: How does the implementation of Freshdesk impact student support workflows?
a: The implementation of Freshdesk showed positive results by providing a centralized knowledge base and ensuring queries are tracked until resolution. This makes the support process more efficient and responsive.

q: What are the functional benefits of a ticketing-based system for an institution?
a: A ticketing-based system enables issue-tracking to ensure no student queries are overlooked and systematizes records of inquiries to make it easier to review students facing graduation issues. It also allows staff to view and correct advice, provides a single reliable source of information, and helps universities provide more efficient student support services. Additionally, workflows are improved by automating repetitive tasks and incorporating a customizable knowledge base.

q: How does a knowledge base function within a ticketing-based system?
a: The knowledge base encourages self-service, which reduces the number of tickets submitted. It allows students to find solutions for themselves and can feature an open forum format where students pitch in their solutions.

q: What is the benefit of having a centralized knowledge base in a ticketing system?
a: A centralized knowledge base and ticketing system can provide accurate, consistent, and up-to-date solutions for academic and administrative concerns with a degree of personalization. It also enables accurate responses and the tracking of student issues.

q: What are the potential consequences of an inadequate student support system in ODeL environments?
a: A support system that fails to meet student needs can impact student retention, success, and completion. Online students require significantly more support than residential or on-campus students.

q: What is the primary purpose of the research conducted by Habito and Sarinas?
a: The research aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the Diploma and Master of Environment and Natural Resources Management (MENRM) program at the University of the Philippines Open University. It specifically assesses if the program successfully builds the capacity of professionals for career advancement and environmental advocacy.

q: What were the main findings regarding the professional impact of the MENRM program on graduates?
a: The program contributed to graduates' personal and professional development, specifically through increased capacity for project and people management, policy making, and improved research, technical, and critical thinking skills. Additionally, the tracer study showed that successful completion of the program can be attributed to an increase in graduates' work responsibility and compensation.

q: What methodology did the researchers use to evaluate the MENRM program?
a: The researchers employed a mixed-methods approach. This involved analyzing admission data from 534 applicants and conducting an online tracer study with 29 graduates from school years 2010-2014.

q: What specific area of the MENRM curriculum was identified as needing improvement?
a: The study found that communication skills need to be better addressed in the program. Only 38% of graduates felt the program "very much" improved their communication skills, which is lower than other competency ratings.

q: What are the key conclusions regarding the role of the MENRM program in professional development?
a: The MENRM program serves as a successful catalyst for career advancement and increased professional responsibility. It fulfills its mission of capacity-building through the open and distance e-learning modality.

q: Who are the primary demographics of the MENRM applicants?
a: Most applicants are working professionals, with 91% being employed in private institutions or government offices. Most are located in the Philippines, specifically in Metro Manila and South Luzon.

q: How does the MENRM program structure allow for different levels of completion?
a: The program utilizes a ladderized system with two exits. Students can earn a Diploma after 24 units or a Master's degree after 27 units, research courses, and a capstone project.

q: What are the implications of strengthening environmental communication in the curriculum?
a: Strengthening communication skills would help graduates translate scientific research into actionable information. This is necessary to influence public perception and policy regarding environmental sustainability.

q: What were the primary motivations for applicants to enroll in the MENRM program?
a: Applicants were primarily motivated by the desire to enhance their knowledge and skills. They also valued the flexibility of the ODeL format and the program's relevance to their current employment.

q: How does the MENRM program influence the professional roles of its graduates?
a: The program contributes to graduates' ability to take on policy-making roles and increased technical responsibility. It also enhances their capacity for people management and professional decision-making.

q: How is the MENRM program structured to accommodate different student needs?
a: The program uses a ladderized design that offers two exits: a Diploma and a Master's degree. This allows students to progress through 24 units for a diploma or 27 units plus research for a master's.

q: What specific skill gap was identified through the assessment of graduate outcomes?
a: The assessment revealed a need to strengthen program components pertaining to communication skills. It was noted that the development of communication skills needs to be targeted, better addressed, and enriched as a required 21st century skill.

q: In what ways does the MENRM program build the capacity of environmental professionals?
a: The program enhances technical skills, research abilities, and critical thinking. It also builds confidence in independent learning and management competencies.

q: How does the program impact the economic capacity of its graduates?
a: Completion of the program is linked to increased compensation for many graduates. Specifically, 55% of respondents reported receiving higher salaries after finishing the degree.

q: What benefit does the ODeL format provide to the target demographic of the MENRM program?
a: The ODeL format provides flexibility in terms of time and remote access. It also allows ease of access to higher institutions of learning for professionals and adult learners.

q: Where are the majority of MENRM applicants located?
a: Most applicants are based in the Philippines. They are specifically concentrated in Metro Manila and South Luzon.

q: What methodology was used to support the different stakeholders in the project?
a: The project manager created a philosophy stating, "we will achieve this project for all learners, for lecturers and staff." In accordance with this philosophy, production tools and media literacy instructional materials were developed.

q: What are the key conclusions regarding the factors necessary for project success?
a: The most important factor is a philosophy that aims to achieve the project for all learners, lecturers, and staff. Additionally, a trust relationship between lecturers and staff is necessary, as technological ability alone cannot motivate staff to develop good productions.

q: Who does the Smart Lecture Video Production method matter to?
a: The Smart Lecture Video Production method matters to all learners, lecturers, and staff. This includes providing high-quality content for learners, including people with disabilities, a comfortable studio environment for natural lecturing, and a streamlined skill improvement process for staff.

q: How were accessibility needs for learners addressed in the production process?
a: A closed caption display function was developed for the video player to allow for the display of captions in various sizes and colors. This function can read both SubRip and WebVTT formats and is compatible with personal computers and tablets like the iPad.

q: How did the project define the role of instructional designers?
a: The instructional designer (IDer) is selected from the faculty. Additionally, an online course team must include an IDer from a different field’s faculty to provide peer review for the lecturing professor to ensure lectures are easy to understand.

q: How was the Moodle video player utilized to support learners?
a: A closed caption display function was developed for the video player to display captions in 23 characters and three lines at the bottom of the video frame. These captions can be displayed on personal computers and tablets, such as iPads, and can have adjustable character sizes and colors to differentiate speakers.

q: What role did automated tools play in the production workflow?
a: A script sheet generating tool was developed using PowerPoint macro to facilitate the script preparation process. This tool can automatically color-code scripts for multiple lecturers and includes a time prediction function that automatically calculates the time required for each section.

q: How did the project support lecturers in delivering fluent video lectures?
a: The project developed a prompter tool using PowerPoint macro that enables scripts to be displayed in the PowerPoint note area on the prompter. This allows lecturers to read material while looking into the camera, solving the difficulty of simultaneously changing slides and turning the pages of a paper script.

q: What was the guiding philosophy established for the production project?
a: The guiding philosophy was: 'we will achieve this project for all learners, for lecturers and staff.' This mission-driven approach guided the development of all tools and training.

q: How did the project's philosophy influence the production outcomes?
a: In accordance with the philosophy, production tools and media literacy instructional materials were developed. As a result, the project mission was accomplished.

q: How were physical spaces adapted for the video production process?
a: Renovated warehouse spaces were utilized as studios for the lecturers. This provided a dedicated environment for creating the online course content.

q: What tools were used to streamline the creation of production scripts?
a: A 'Script Sheet Generating Tool' was developed using PowerPoint macros. This tool allowed staff to automatically generate detailed scripts and time predictions from presentation notes.

q: How did the project address the need for media literacy in staff training?
a: In accordance with the philosophy to achieve the project for all learners, lecturers, and staff, media literacy instructional materials were developed. These materials were created alongside production tools as part of the Smart Lecture Video Production method.

q: What are the different classifications of video lectures used at the Open University of Japan?
a: Video lectures are classified into six types: straight talk, talk, location, interview, experiment/simulation, and language skit. These can be further divided into lectures that include inserted video or those that do not.

q: What is the central purpose of the research conducted at the RGO Review Center?
a: The research aims to examine student perceptions of a pilot distance education program for the psychometrician review. It specifically seeks to understand student satisfaction within an online learning environment for professional licensure preparation.

q: What were the main findings regarding why students chose distance education?
a: The primary motivation for choosing distance education was the flexibility of time and location at 69.6%. Other significant reasons included work commitments at 52.2% and family commitments at 34.8%.

q: What research method was used to gather data from the psychometrician review students?
a: The researcher employed a survey research method using a questionnaire partially adopted from Alam et al. (2012). The survey was distributed through an exclusive Facebook group containing the enrolled students.

q: What are the practical recommendations for improving distance learning in review centers?
a: Practical recommendations include establishing a learning schedule that segregates files by week, providing prompt feedback through self-grading assessments, and allowing lecturers to provide downloadable, read-only materials. Additionally, group discussions should occur even in asynchronous forms, and learner support regarding registration, successful distance learning, and transferring should be clear.

q: How did the RGO Review Center deliver its online psychometrician review program?
a: The program utilized a combination of print-based materials and online delivery via Facebook. This delivery included live and recorded video lectures, review notes, mock examinations, and answer keys.

q: How does the Commission on Higher Education define review centers?
a: CHED defines review centers as hubs offering programs intended to refresh and enhance the knowledge, competencies, and skills of students. These programs prepare students for upcoming licensure examinations given by bodies such as the Professional Regulation Commission.

q: What technological factor enabled the distribution of knowledge for distance learning in review centers?
a: Technological advances have led to the distribution of knowledge using internet-enabled services. This has allowed review centers to offer open and distance learning alongside their brick-and-mortar classes.

q: What was the student experience regarding group discussions in the online program?
a: There was no group discussion aside from student-prompted questions. The review program did not formally include any group discussion or points of interaction between lecturers and students, but it provided an avenue for students to ask and receive answers from lecturers.

q: What was the student perception regarding the promptness of instructor feedback?
a: The group of respondents was torn towards receiving prompt feedback as this is subjective. Only 12 respondents agreed that feedback was prompt, while 11 respondents were either neutral or disagreed, as exams were given upon enrollment but feedback was provided after a few months.

q: How did students perceive the learning materials provided in the distance learning program?
a: Most respondents found the learning materials to be self-explanatory. The use of the internet was also noted to have increased among the students.

q: What was the primary motivation for students to enroll in the distance education program?
a: The primary motivation was the flexibility of time and location, cited by 69.6% of respondents. This was followed by work commitments and family commitments.

q: How did the RGO Review Center implement its open and distance learning pilot in 2018?
a: The center offered a home-based study program delivered online. This program utilized Facebook to provide video lectures, review notes, and mock examinations.

q: How is distance education defined by Simonson, Smaldino, Albright, and Zvacek (2008)?
a: Distance education is defined as education having a distance. This distance can be geographical, time, or even intellectual.

q: What characterizes synchronous distance education?
a: Synchronous distance education is delivered through media that allows communication at the same time. Examples include video conferencing, long-distance calling, and chatting.

q: What are the four generations of open and distance learning in the Philippines according to Bandalaria (2007)?
a: The generations include radio technology, print-based materials with radio or face-to-face classes, print-based materials with pre-recorded audio or video, and internet-based affordances like chats and discussion forums. These generations are characterized by different technological advancements within each epoch.

q: What factors affect student satisfaction in distance education according to Sahin and Shelley (2008)?
a: Student satisfaction is affected by computer knowledge and attitudinal factors. If computer knowledge is inadequate, students might not be satisfied with the quality and appropriateness of the education.

q: What role does faculty motivation play in the success of a distance education program according to Schifter (2002)?
a: Faculty members contribute to the success of a distance education program when they are motivated by intrinsic motivations. An example of such motivation is job satisfaction.

q: What is the main proposal of this research?
a: The paper proposes applying a modified Facebook engagement rate formula to Moodle to measure student engagement with forum posts. This approach aims to identify which specific topics or posts drive the most interaction in the learning process.

q: What were the results of the simulation using dummy data?
a: After feeding dummy data into the modified Moodle post engagement rate formula, it was concluded that it is possible to aggregate data using an existing social media formula and apply it to an online course. This collected data can be used to gain insights and measure student interaction and engagement with Moodle posts.

q: What are the key conclusions regarding the use of social media formulas in education?
a: Applying a social media engagement formula to an online course may provide instructors and educational institutions with valuable feedback on which posts, comments, or topics increase student interaction. This exercise could lead to new metrics that help distance learning institutions calibrate content to improve student engagement with instructors, peers, and the course.

q: Who can benefit from implementing these engagement metrics?
a: Instructors can use these metrics to understand student interaction, while educational institutions can use them to calibrate course content. This can ultimately improve interaction between students, instructors, and the online course.

q: What are the broader implications for the design of online curricula?
a: Applying an existing social media audience engagement formula to an online course may provide instructors and educational institutions valuable feedback on what types of posts, comments, or topics make students interact and engage more. This exercise could help educational institutions improve course and content design by discovering which types of content achieve higher student engagement rates in learning management systems.

q: How does the definition of 'Reach' in this model differ from total enrollment?
a: Reach is defined specifically as the unique number of students who actually viewed a specific forum post. It is not based on the total number of students enrolled in the course.

q: How does this research relate to the field of learning analytics?
a: This research proposes applying a modified Facebook engagement rate formula to Moodle to measure student engagement with forum posts and identify which topics engage them more. This approach may provide valuable feedback to instructors and lead to new metrics for improving student interaction and engagement in online learning sessions.

q: What is the goal of using these metrics to improve the student experience?
a: The goal is to provide feedback on what types of posts, comments, or topics make students interact and engage more in online learning sessions. This may allow institutions to calibrate content to improve student interaction and engagement with instructors, fellow students, and the online course in general.

q: How is the Facebook engagement rate formula adapted for Moodle?
a: The formula is adapted by using Moodle's log and usage reports to track activities similar to clicks, comments, and likes, though

q: What specific Facebook metrics are used in the Moodle Post Engagement Rate?
a: The formula utilizes clicks, comments, and likes to measure engagement. These are divided by the unique number of students who viewed the post to determine the rate.

q: In what way does the research bridge social media and education?
a: The research proposes marrying Moodle's data logs with social media calculation methods. This allows educators to use proven social media metrics to understand student interaction depth.

q: What tools can instructors use to derive learning analytics for their courses?
a: Instructors can use built-in analytics and reporting tools within learning management systems like Moodle and Blackboard. They may also use external software such as Microsoft Excel to derive these analytics.

q: How does Facebook define its engagement rate metric?
a: Facebook defines engagement rate as the percentage of people who saw a post that reacted to, shared, clicked, or commented on it. This metric serves as an indicator of the impact content has on an audience.

q: What is the K-Index in the context of academic social media presence?
a: The K-Index is a calculation of an academic's number of Twitter followers divided by the number of followers they are expected to have based on their citation record. A K-index greater than 5 can categorize a researcher as a "Science Kardashian."

q: How does the Klout Score measure social media influence?
a: The Klout Score uses more than 400 signals from eight different social networks to measure influence on a daily basis. It is an accumulation of a person's influence across all social network memberships rather than an average.

q: What is the proposed solution to improve online learning accessibility?
a: The proposed solution is the development of Facebook Classroom, which would feature an inclusive mode to assist learners with visual impairments, hearing impairments, navigation difficulties, and overstimulation issues. Additionally, it is recommended that the government and telecommunication networks provide free data access to accommodate students from different communities.

q: How does Facebook compare to traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS) in terms of student engagement?
a: Students engage more quickly via Facebook Groups because the application is already installed and the interface is familiar compared to traditional LMS platforms.

q: What specific inclusivity features should the proposed Facebook Classroom include?
a: The platform should include specific modes to assist learners with visual, hearing, navigation, or overstimulation issues.

q: Who would benefit most from the implementation of the proposed Facebook Classroom?
a: Marginalized communities, differently-abled learners, and students in the Philippines facing data and storage constraints would benefit most.

q: What are the potential drawbacks or risks of using Facebook for education?
a: Potential challenges include security risks like hacking, student distraction by personal content, and psychological stress from constant notifications.

q: What is the significance of 'ubiquity' in the context of this research?
a: Facebook's ubiquity is seen as the key feature that makes it a viable platform for educational learning environments. This ubiquity, along with its engaging power, provides a foundation to develop Facebook as an online learning space for Filipino learners.

q: What barriers prevent marginalized communities from using traditional OPL platforms?
a: Marginalized communities face barriers such as high costs, application restrictions, and limited access to high-speed internet.

q: What are the limitations of traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS) like Moodle and Blackboard in the Philippine context?
a: In the Philippine context, popular OPL platforms like Moodle and Blackboard pose accessibility and inclusivity issues, particularly for marginalized and differently-abled communities. Additionally, these platforms can be a hassle because students must switch applications to interact with classmates, whereas social media serves as a more frequent medium for communication.

q: How does Facebook Messenger compare to traditional LMS discussion forums?
a: Facebook Messenger proved to be a more efficient medium for quick communication than traditional LMS discussion forums.

q: Why is Facebook considered a viable breeding ground for collaborative learning?
a: Facebook is a pervasive global informational hub and is used extensively by Filipinos, making it a highly accessible medium.

q: What is the current state of online personal learning (OPL) in the Philippines?
a: The use of popular learning platforms is not fully realized in the Philippines due to accessibility and inclusivity concerns.

q: How can e-Learning platforms better serve differently-abled students?
a: Platforms can include specialized modes designed to assist learners with visual impairments, hearing impairments, navigation difficulties, or overstimulation issues.

q: What is the difference between sophisticated LMS tools and actual accessibility for Filipino learners?
a: Popular LMSs or OPL platforms like Blackboard, Moodle, and Edmodo present accessibility and inclusivity concerns, as well as application restrictions. Developing an existing ubiquitous platform like Facebook can better address these issues than building new learning systems, which pose more constraints to different types of educators and learners in the Philippine context.

q: What are the primary functions of a Learning Management System (LMS)?
a: An LMS enables learners to access various course sites and customize their online learning environment. These platforms may also be referred to as online personal learning (OPL) platforms.

q: What honors has the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU) received?
a: CHED considers UPOU the National Center of Excellence in Open and Distance Education. Additionally, the APEC Digital Opportunity Center included its virtual classroom, MyPortal, in the Top 10 Best in e-Practice list.

q: How does the Department of Education (DepEd) prioritize internet connectivity in the Philippines?
a: The government prioritizes providing internet connectivity to remote, far-flung, and poorest "outskirt schools." Currently, only 26% of the 46,000 public schools nationwide have internet access.

q: What is the role of digital literacy in engaging with social networks?
a: Digital literacy is a prerequisite for further engagement in social networks. It involves awareness of different Facebook functions and understanding internet jargon used in online correspondence.

q: What were the main findings regarding the computer self-efficacy of nursing graduate students?
a: The students' computer self-efficacy skills were high in their beginning skills and rated fairly in their advanced skills. They were also very confident in using their computers and had a positive attitude towards learning through the Internet.

q: What was the relationship between computer self-efficacy and attitudes toward e-learning?
a: Statistical analysis revealed no significant relationship between computer self-efficacy skills and attitudes toward e-learning, with a p-value of 0.902. This indicates that a student's positive attitude toward e-learning does not depend on their level of computer confidence.

q: How did the nursing graduate students perceive e-learning?
a: The nursing graduate students had a positive attitude towards e-learning, as indicated by a total mean score of 4.01. They were also very confident in using their computers and maintained a positive attitude towards their learning through the Internet.

q: What research methodology was used to collect data from the 33 MAN students?
a: The respondents were requested to answer a consent form containing socio-demographic questions. They were also required to answer questionnaires on the Computer Self-Efficacy Scale for Adults and Attitude Towards e-Learning.

q: What are the key conclusions regarding students with low technical skills?
a: The study concludes that even students who possess only beginning skills in using computers can still maintain a positive outlook toward their studies. A positive attitude toward e-learning does not require advanced computer self-efficacy.

q: What specific recommendations does the researcher provide for students and programs?
a: It is recommended that students be supported by encouraging them to use the Internet and databases extensively for their studies. Additionally, e-counselling may be put up in the program for students having difficulty with their studies.

q: Who are the primary participants involved in this research?
a: The primary participants involved in this research are Master of Arts in Nursing graduate students. These students were studied regarding their computer self-efficacy and attitudes towards e-learning.

q: What are the definitions of computer self-efficacy and attitude in this context?
a: Computer self-efficacy is defined as a judgment of one's capability to use a computer. Attitude is defined as a tendency to react favorably or unfavorably toward a stimulus.

q: What support mechanism is suggested to help students facing difficulties in their studies?
a: E-counselling may be put up in the program for students having difficulty with their studies.

q: How has the adoption of online teaching and learning impacted education accessibility at UPOU?
a: The adoption of online teaching and learning at the University of the Philippines Open University has made education more accessible to students using the Internet.

q: What components are included in the blended learning model used by the MAN program?
a: The MAN program incorporates discussion forums, online quizzes, exams, and face-to-face clinical practicums. This model is part of the University of the Philippines Open University's approach to online teaching.

q: How do students view the utility of e-learning for their professional development?
a: Students' view in e-learning depended on two attitudes: a positive affective attitude when e-learning served as a useful tool through webpage design, and a negative affective attitude attributed to the difficulty to cope up. Additionally, e-learning is rated as useful for the improvement of continuing education with a score of 4.77.

q: What was the mean score for student attitudes toward e-learning?
a: The students demonstrated a highly positive attitude toward e-learning, yielding a total mean score of 4.01.

q: Is there a significant link between how students feel about e-learning and their computer skills?
a: There is no significant relationship between computer self-efficacy skills and attitudes toward e-learning, with a p-value of 0.902. This means a positive attitude does not necessarily depend on a student's level of computer confidence.

q: How do nursing graduate students rate their ability to perform complex computer tasks?
a: The nursing graduate students' computer self-efficacy skills were high in their beginning skills and rated fairly in their advanced skills. The results suggest that the students are not fully confident in using their computers or are not fully familiar with the intricacies of using their computers.

q: How are computer self-efficacy skills categorized for the participants?
a: Computer self-efficacy skills are interpreted as beginning, advanced, and mainframe skills. The results show students have high beginning skills and fair advanced skills.

q: What is the main finding regarding the relationship between self-regulation and online learning self-efficacy?
a: There is a statistically significant and strong positive association between nursing students' self-regulation and online learning self-efficacy. This indicates that as a student's capacity for self-regulation increases, their confidence in succeeding in online learning also tends to increase.

q: What were the specific levels of self-regulation and online learning self-efficacy found in the sample?
a: Nursing students demonstrated moderate levels of self-regulation with a mean of 54.75. They also showed moderate levels of online learning self-efficacy with a mean of 93.01.

q: Who was the target population for this research?
a: The study focused on 166 nursing students aged 18 to 50 attending various nursing colleges in Pampanga, Philippines. This group was chosen because nursing students are particularly vulnerable to stressors due to the competitive nature of their programs.

q: What are the key recommendations for educators and academic administrators based on the results?
a: Academic administration and nurse educators should explore the dynamics between self-regulation and online self-efficacy. They are encouraged to develop specific programs and interventions designed to enhance both of these skills.

q: What are the implications of the findings for nursing students' academic performance?
a: The findings suggest that nursing students should develop an active awareness of their own self-regulation and online self-efficacy. Doing so can help improve their academic performance and independence in digital learning environments.

q: How does self-regulation impact the way nursing students engage with their studies?
a: Self-regulated learners are more likely to set goals and monitor their progress. This behavior helps them develop the confidence needed to navigate the social and technological demands of online education.

q: What role does online learning self-efficacy play in a student's experience?
a: Online learning self-efficacy refers to a student's beliefs and confidence in their ability to complete or engage in specific tasks required of online learners. This confidence is strongly linked to a student's capacity for self-regulation.

q: How can academic administration support students facing the challenges of online instruction?
a: Academic administration and nurse educators should explore the dynamics between self-regulation (SR) and online learning self-efficacy (OLSE) and develop programs that may improve these two variables.

q: What prompted the shift toward online learning for students?
a: The COVID-19 pandemic caused the suspension of face-to-face classes worldwide. This necessitated a global transition to online learning environments, requiring students to adapt to self-directed settings.

q: What specific components of online learning are assessed by the OLSES scale?
a: The Online Learning Self-Efficacy Scale assesses learning in the online environment, time management, and technology use. These factors are critical for success in digital education.

q: What is the relationship between self-efficacy and self-regulation in online settings?
a: There is a statistically significant and strong positive association between the two variables. As a student's capacity for self-regulation increases, their confidence in their ability to succeed in online tasks also tends to increase.

q: Why is understanding self-efficacy important for nursing students specifically?
a: Nursing students are particularly vulnerable to stressors due to the competitive nature of their programs. Understanding their perceived efficacy is essential for their academic success and motivation.

q: What are the common challenges students encounter when transitioning to online learning?
a: Students frequently face difficulties adjusting learning styles and managing poor communication due to a lack of clear instructor directions. Other challenges include poor internet connections and the difficulty of managing household responsibilities while attending online classes.

q: How does the Self-regulation Questionnaire measure self-regulation?
a: The Self-regulation Questionnaire consists of 63 items that assess seven specific dimensions. These dimensions include information input, self-evaluation, instigation to change, search for change, planning for change, implementation of strategies for change, and goal attainment evaluation plan.

q: What is the relationship between self-efficacy and self-regulated learning behaviors?
a: Self-efficacy and self-regulated learning have significant meaningful correlations and influence each other positively. Students with high self-efficacy are more likely to engage in setting goals, monitoring learning, performing strategies, and evaluating progress.

q: What were the main findings regarding the cost difference between the traditional and OER models?
a: The traditional model for a Microeconomics course cost RM97,103 over four semesters, whereas the OER model reduced the total cost to RM6,987.50. This transition resulted in total university savings of approximately RM1.4 million by mid-2016.

q: How did the researcher investigate the impact of OER on course development?
a: The researcher employed a descriptive case study methodology focusing on the revision of a Microeconomics course. This involved comparing the costs and stakeholder roles of the traditional model against a revised model utilizing OER.

q: What are the key conclusions regarding the use of OER in distance learning?
a: Using OER fits into the philosophy of ensuring the costs of course and program development are kept low so that tuition fees would not increase. This aligns with the goal of making education accessible to all.

q: What are the primary limitations or challenges identified in using OER?
a: Challenges include low acceptance among academics for course development or revision purposes and difficulties in determining the quality of resources used. Additionally, content creators may hold back on contributions because OER can be a source of income for some.

q: What are the implications for future research in this field?
a: Future research should focus on the sustainability and viability of OER and its direct impact on student learning capabilities. There is also a need for more studies regarding student feedback on the learning experience when using fully localized OER.

q: What specific costs were eliminated by adopting the OER model?
a: Adopting the OER model minimized the cost in sourcing for content because there is no need to purchase textbooks or pay fees for copyrighted materials.

q: How does the use of OER align with the mission of Open and Distance Learning (ODL) institutions?
a: OER supports the ODL mission by significantly reducing costs, which helps keep tuition fees low. This reduction in cost helps make education more accessible to all students.

q: What was the traditional course development approach used by Wawasan Open University?
a: Wawasan Open University relies on the development of custom-designed course materials with self-instructional properties using commissioned writers. These materials are usually developed as an adaptation of textbooks or licensed course materials from other institutions.

q: How did the OER model change the development timeline and process for distance learning courses?
a: The study used a Microeconomics course to show how OER can replace traditional textbooks and licensed courseware. This shift helps address the financial pressure faced by ODL institutions due to escalating content creation costs.

q: How much money did Wawasan Open University save through OER implementation?
a: The project saved the university a total of RM1.4 million, which is approximately US$350,000, by mid-2016. This was achieved by replacing textbooks and licensed coursewares with OER.

q: What are the specific formats in which OER are delivered to learners?
a: OER are included in course delivery in the form of videos, podcasts, and supplementary materials. These additional resources help improve learner comprehension in meeting course learning outcomes.

q: How often does Wawasan Open University revise its course content?
a: Wawasan Open University implements a five-year currency of knowledge. Every five years, faculty members begin revising the content of their respective courses as part of a university-wide exercise.

q: What are the potential costs associated with using OER?
a: While OER is free, the adaptation work required may involve costs. However, the adaptation of the original resource is expected and allowed, making the end price for learners negligible.
