a: The modules are divided into R-Modules for administrative functions, I-Modules for tenure, teaching effectiveness, and student counseling, and T-Modules for liberal arts values, teaching strategies, and innovative technologies. These categories cover reception, information, and teaching needs.

q: Who is the primary target audience for this faculty development resource?
a: The resource is designed to support new faculty members, particularly those transitioning from large research-oriented universities to liberal arts institutions. It is also intended to serve as a potential resource for the broader academic community.

q: What are the limitations identified in the evaluation of the website?
a: Design and layout improvements were necessary to make the website more navigable, and one participant experienced difficulty navigating some of the links. Additionally, the website needed a Japanese translation to reflect the bilingual nature of the university.

q: Under what license was the faculty development website released?
a: The website was released through a Creative Commons license. All pages on the website contain the Creative Commons License information of CC-BY-NC 3.0.

q: What delivery modes were utilized to ensure the accessibility of the program?
a: The program utilized blended, online, and mobile delivery modes. This included face-to-face sessions supported by Moodle, a website with reading and video resources, and a mobile app providing text, audio, and video.

q: How was the faculty development website classified in terms of educational resource type?
a: The website was reported as an Open Educational Resource (OER). Its materials are provided through a Creative Commons license, specifically CC-BY-NC 3.0.

q: What delivery modes were implemented to support the accessibility of the OER?
a: The program used blended, online, and mobile delivery modes to ensure accessibility. These modes included a website, a mobile app, and face-to-face sessions supported by Moodle.

q: What specific pedagogical challenges do new faculty face in East Asian liberal arts institutions?
a: New faculty trained at large research universities often struggle to adapt to the specific pedagogical requirements of liberal arts education. This is exacerbated in East Asia where research orientation often takes precedence over teaching.

q: What specific content was included to support liberal arts values?
a: The program includes T-Modules that focus specifically on liberal arts values and teaching strategies. These modules were developed following a needs assessment of the ICU community.

q: Why is there an urgent need for specialized support in liberal arts settings at ICU?
a: There was an urgent need to support new faculty in understanding liberal arts values and balancing professional responsibilities with well-being. This is particularly important for those coming from research-heavy university backgrounds.

q: What tools were used to build the online faculty development website?
a: The website was built using Google Sites. It contains various reading and video resources to support learning.

q: How was the usability of the online materials measured?
a: Usability was measured using the System Usability Scale (SUS), which yielded an average score of 73. Researchers also used questions adapted from the Technology Acceptance Model to measure perceived ease of use.

q: What are the potential benefits of faculty development programs for students and faculty?
a: Faculty development programs can have positive effects on student achievement and satisfaction. They also contribute to the wellbeing of faculty members.

q: What methodology was used to investigate the communication tools within the UPOU MODeL platform?
a: The researchers employed a descriptive content analysis of inquiries received through the MODeL LMS, Gmail, and a Facebook Page during 2017 and 2018. These inquiries were categorized by theme and classified into administrative, technical, instructional, and counseling and tutorial support.

q: What categories of learner support were identified in the analysis of inquiries?
a: Inquiries were categorized according to the type of learner support: administrative, technical, instructional, and counseling and tutorial support. These categories were based on Keast (1997).

q: How does the UPOU MODeL platform relate to the mission of the University of the Philippines Open University?
a: The MODeL platform is part of the university's mission to provide wider access to quality higher education. This initiative responds to the Open Distance Learning Law (Republic Act 10650) by offering free online courses.

q: What were the most common types of inquiries received through the Facebook Page in 2018?
a: In 2018, 61.7% of the inquiries sent through the Facebook Page were related to Registration and Enrollment. This indicates that students primarily use Facebook for administrative-related matters.

q: How does the UPOU MODeL platform facilitate access to higher education?
a: The platform provides free online courses to a wider audience, promoting equity and flexibility in the learning environment. This supports the university's mission to provide wider access to quality higher education.

q: Which communication tools are most effective for providing counseling and tutorial support?
a: Email is the preferred medium for students seeking counseling and tutorial support regarding course details, materials, and certificates. This channel accounted for 60% of all counseling and tutorial inquiries.

q: What are the defining characteristics of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs)?
a: MOOCs are characterized by being massive, accessible everywhere online, open to everyone, and free of charge. They are considered disruptive technologies in higher education.

q: How do MOOCs contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the Education 2030 Framework for Action?
a: MOOCs help address international development agendas by tackling exclusion and inequalities in access, participation, and learning outcomes. They provide flexibility and equity to individuals denied education based on factors like race, religion, gender, or socio-economic status.

q: What are the typical components of a web-based MOOC?
a: MOOCs are web-based courses held by professors or experts through video lectures, computer-graded tests, and discussion forums. They originated from the open educational resources (OER) movement.

q: When and by whom was the first known MOOC created?
a: The first known MOOC was created by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) OpenCourseware in 2002. Its purpose was to provide free web access to MIT course materials.

q: What are the potential benefits of MOOCs for higher education institutions and students?
a: MOOCs can offer educational benefits to professors, students, and higher education institutes. They are praised for bringing elite institutional opportunities to a wider audience and addressing rising higher education costs.

q: What are the twelve factors identified in the context of MOOCs?
a: The factors include degree of openness, scale of participation, use of multimedia, degree of communication, degree of collaboration, learning pathway, quality assurance, amount of reflection, certification, formal learning, autonomy, and diversity.

q: How many courses has the UPOU MODeL platform offered since its inception?
a: The UPOU Massive Open and Distance eLearning (UPOU MODeL) has offered a total of 84 courses since it started.

q: What specific certification programs have been offered through UPOU MODeL?
a: Certification programs offered include Technology for Teaching and Learning, ODeL Teacher Accreditation, Business Analytics, and Sustainable Development. Other programs include ASEAN Studies, eFilipiniana, and Interlocal Cooperation.

q: What is the distinction between learner support and student support?
a: Student support is often referred to as tutoring, whereas learner support is referred to as administrative and personal support. Learner support is defined as the totality of institutional provision to a learner, excluding generic teaching materials.

q: What are the four types of learner support identified by Keast?
a: The four types are administrative, technical, instructional, and counseling and tutorial support. These range from organizational activities like registration to providing academic assistance and guidance.

q: What specific activities are included under administrative learner support?
a: Administrative support includes admissions, registration, course scheduling, student records, and financial transactions. These activities ensure the operation of the institution or program.

q: What was the primary goal of the UPOUDC Digital Collective project?
a: The project aimed to practice student co-creation of multimedia content, such as stock photographs, graphics, and audio. The objective was to build an online community and produce open educational resources for the wider UPOU learning community.

q: What were the main findings regarding the failure of the co-creation project?
a: The project failed due to a lack of interaction and engagement necessary for co-creation and community development. Findings indicated that cultural influences, such as fear of embarrassment and a need for established hierarchy, contributed to this lack of success.

q: How did the cultural trait of 'hiya' affect student participation?
a: In online student interaction, students tend to disengage rather than risk embarrassment to themselves and the disappointment of peers and mentors. Hiya was also highlighted as a factor detrimental to student engagement and interaction, potentially stemming from feelings of insecurity or inferiority towards older and more knowledgeable peers.

q: What conclusions were drawn regarding the relationship between technology and engagement?
a: The technology employed did not exacerbate the situation, but it is in a position to be of more help in fostering a higher level of interaction. Student engagement was found to be a constant issue with several causes, including shifting priorities and behavior influenced by the prevailing culture among participants.

q: What is the distinction between a 'pseudo community' and a 'true community' in this context?
a: A pseudo community's essential dynamic is conflict avoidance, whereas a true community's essential dynamic is conflict-resolution. This implies that for a true community, conflict must occur in order to be resolved.

q: How did Filipino cultural traits specifically hinder student engagement in the project?
a: The fear of embarrassment and a perceived need to avoid conflict are ingrained in Filipino culture and must be addressed for engagement to prosper. Additionally, some participants exhibited ningas cogon, a trait where initial enthusiasm gradually diminishes over time to the point of indifference.

q: What methods were suggested to improve the sense of achievement and confidence for learners?
a: Recognition and credit are valued by some community members and can help build confidence. These were originally intended to be provided through attribution to co-created content.

q: What was the intended output for the open educational resources (OERs) being created?
a: The project aimed to produce shared stock photographs, graphics, and audio. These resources were intended to be shared with the wider University of the Philippines Open University learning community.

q: What are the specific activities that can be considered co-creation between students and staff in higher education?
a: Co-creation activities include participation in university governance and the co-creation of marketing materials. These activities are part of a working model proposed by Dollinger and Lodge (2019).

q: What factors influence the cultural landscape of the Philippines?
a: The Philippines is influenced by multiple cultures through colonization by Spain, the United States, and Japan, as well as contact with the Chinese and Malay races. Colonization also acted as a catalyst for bridging cultures through Christianity or Americanized education.

q: What is the cultural divide described by Enriquez regarding the Filipino population?
a: Enriquez cited a cultural divide between the Filipino masses and the elites. This is manifested by their tendency to adapt either popular or traditional culture, which are typically opposed to one another.

q: What is missing from the Dollinger and Lodge (2019) framework regarding co-creation?
a: The framework does not include culture as a factor for positive outcome, either as a barrier or value-in-use. Additionally, there is a lack of focus on communities of practice as a support system for co-creation.

q: What research methods were used to gather data from the co-creation project participants?
a: A semi-structured interview was conducted with willing participants, with a preference for real-time group discussions. Participants were also given the option to answer an online questionnaire.

q: Which digital platforms were used to facilitate the Digital Collective co-creation initiative?
a: Communication was facilitated through Facebook (via a Page, a closed group, and Messenger), a WordPress site, and Slack. These technologies were used to help members as part of the community and as UPOU students.

q: How many participants were involved in the Digital Collective co-creation initiative research?
a: A total of nine participants were involved, consisting of six people who answered the questionnaire and three who opted for interviews. These participants represented both core members and less active members.

q: How were the participants categorized based on their activity levels in the project?
a: Five participants were identified as core members who were highly active in communicating and coordinating. The other four were less active members who mostly engaged in lurking or occasional posting.

q: What value did participants find in the co-creation project?
a: Participants valued the community and camaraderie, specifically the friendships built over the time spent on the project. They also suggested that participants value earning recognition or credit for their efforts.

q: What was the consensus among participants regarding culture and the co-creation project?
a: All study participants reached a consensus that culture affects the co-creation project and the development of a community of practice. Some participants also believed the project members possessed cultural diversity.

q: What is the primary purpose of the research conducted at Nueva Vizcaya State University?
a: The research investigates the preparedness of incoming freshmen for online and distance education (OLDE). It specifically examines technological competence, self-directed learning abilities, and attitudes toward e-learning.

q: What are the main findings regarding student readiness for online and distance education?
a: Graduating students from the ABM track are generally prepared for online and distance education. They demonstrate competence in offline, mobile, and internet-based technologies and possess favorable attitudes toward e-learning.

q: How do technological activities correlate with student attitudes toward learning?
a: There is a very significant and positive correlation between offline computer-based technology activities and attitudes toward learning. Additionally, mobile internet and internet-based activities also show significant positive correlations with attitudes toward e-learning.

q: What are the key recommendations for the university administration?
a: The researcher recommends investing in ICT infrastructure, transitioning up to 25 percent of contact hours to online modalities, and implementing a staggered transition to e-learning via a University-wide Learning Management System.

q: What are the implications for the university's strategic goals?
a: The findings support the university's goal to become a premier provider of high-quality Open Distance Education (ODE) programs and a dual-mode institution. The data helps determine if students are prepared to transition from traditional campus-based environments to digital offerings.

q: What are the limitations regarding the relationship between internet access and readiness?
a: The study found no significant overall correlations between students' internet access, both inside and outside the university, and their self-directed learning, control, or attitudes toward e-learning.

q: What are the attitudes of students toward e-learning?
a: The graduating students from the ABM track demonstrated favorable overall attitudes toward e-learning. These attitudes are significantly correlated with mobile internet and internet-based activities.

q: How do students perform in terms of self-directed learning?
a: Students were rated as being 'often' self-directed in their learning and control. There is a significant positive correlation between internet-based activities and these self-directed learning abilities.

q: How does this research support the university's strategic goals?
a: The research supports the goal of becoming a premier provider of high-quality Open Distance Education (ODE) programs. It also assists the university in its aim to become a dual-mode institution.

q: What transition strategy is suggested for implementing distance education?
a: The researcher suggests a staggered transition to e-learning via a University-wide Learning Management System. This would involve a dedicated project team to manage planning and technical requirements.

q: Are students prepared for the transition to online and distance education?
a: Graduating students from the SHS ABM Track have favorable overall attitudes towards e-learning and are ready for online and distance education. They are also rated as competent in the use of offline computer-based, mobile-based, and internet-based technologies.

q: How competent are students in using offline computer-based technologies?
a: Students were rated as competent in the use of offline computer-based technologies. There is a very significant and positive correlation between these activities and attitudes toward learning.

q: What role do mobile and internet-based technologies play in student competence?
a: Students were rated as competent in both mobile-based and internet-based technologies. Significant positive correlations were found between mobile internet activity and attitudes toward e-learning.

q: What specific student group participated in the survey regarding online and distance education readiness?
a: The survey included 38 graduating students from the Accountancy, Business and Management Track of the Nueva Vizcaya State University College of Teacher Education Senior High School program. These students were assessed using a researcher-developed questionnaire.

q: What is the general perception of students regarding their internet access outside the university?
a: Students reported that their internet access outside the university is open but very limited, receiving a score of 2 out of 4 on the Likert scale. This limited access applies to utilizing personal data, university Wi-Fi, cyber cafés, computer laboratories, and cable internet services.

q: What is the primary problem addressed by the development of the Online Advisory Committee (AdCom) App?
a: The app addresses the difficulties faced by students, faculty members, and support staff in designating an advisory committee for each student. It aims to provide a more efficient and substantial systemic change in academic advising processes, specifically regarding record-keeping, faculty load management, human error reduction, and response immediacy.

q: What methodology was used to develop the AdCom App?
a: The Iterative Incremental Model was employed as a framework for the development of the application. The process involved identifying user categories and system requirements, followed by Analysis, Design, Coding, and Software Iterations.

q: What are the key conclusions regarding the use of the AdCom App compared to manual practices?
a: The AdCom App offers a more convenient, sustainable, and paperless method of student support. It maximizes available resources through technology-enabled advising and improves the efficiency of academic and administrative processes.

q: Who will benefit most from the implementation of this automated advising system?
a: The system is intended for enrolled students to use early in the semester. Additionally, the development of the app aims to provide better services for students and improve the consultation system of faculty members.

q: What are the broader implications of implementing automated advising in Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) contexts?
a: The implementation of this practice would augment the student-adviser relationship in UPOU and contribute to the development of an efficient academic advising system in other HEIs.

q: What technical architecture supports the AdCom App?
a: The system utilizes PHP 7.0.30, the Laravel Framework 5.5, and a MySQL database. It also incorporates Supervisor for email monitoring, Crontab for link expiration, and DomPDF for document generation.

q: How does the AdCom App ensure equitable faculty workloads?
a: The app implements a "quota" filter in the system that takes into consideration the availability and load equity among the faculty members. This quota system is determined by the number of active students over the number of advisers.

q: What specific recommendation is made to optimize the matching between students and advisers?
a: The researchers suggest the potential integration of the Gale-Shapley 'Stable Matching' algorithm. This would help ensure the most apt matching between a student's research topic and an adviser's specialization.

q: How does the AdCom App improve the process of forming academic committees for students?
a: The AdCom App enables students to select their advisory committee online and familiarize themselves with faculty members through photos, names, and research interests. It also allows faculty to accept or decline nominations via automated email, implements a quota filter for availability and load equity, and automatically generates Form 1 for record-keeping.

q: In what way does the AdCom App provide a more sustainable form of student support?
a: The paperless record-keeping system allows for a more sustainable practice.

q: What specific software tools are used to power the AdCom App platform?
a: The platform is built using the Laravel Framework 5.5 and a MySQL database. It also employs DomPDF for generating official documents and Supervisor for monitoring emails.

q: What are the primary responsibilities of an academic adviser?
a: An adviser assists their advisee in identifying the specific courses to be taken throughout a program curriculum. Additionally, the adviser works with panel members to help devise and refine the student's thesis or dissertation.

q: Which specific programs at UPOU FICS require students to select an adviser and panel committee?
a: The requirement applies to the Doctor of Communication (DComm), Master of Development Communication (MDC), and Bachelor of Arts in Multimedia Studies (BAMS) programs. Students in these programs must choose faculty members who possess expertise aligned with their research interests.

q: How did the DComm and MDC programs previously facilitate the nomination of advisers and panel members?
a: These programs formerly conducted a face-to-face topic presentation every semester. This physical meeting was intended to facilitate the nomination process for students.

q: What was the previous method used by BAMS faculty to appoint student advisers?
a: BAMS faculty members used to meet physically to appoint advisers. This was based on the specific topics that students submitted through the system.

q: What design considerations were prioritized during the creation of the AdCom App interface?
a: The interface layout was designed to be user-friendly and straightforward. This was intended to accommodate a diverse range of users, including Millennials, Generation X, and Baby Boomers.

q: What were the main benefits identified by instructors using the flipped learning model?
a: The implementation of flipped learning helped save time spent on online instruction, offered learners a chance to control their learnings, and helped students at different levels. Additionally, instructors found it allowed for more student-instructor interaction and helped them understand their students better.

q: What were the primary challenges encountered during the implementation of this model?
a: Significant challenges included an added workload for instructors due to preparation and grading, as well as extra work for students which can lead to low motivation and lack of participation. Additionally, students faced difficulty adapting to the active learning required by the flipped classroom, a challenge exacerbated by the novelty of the online setting.

q: How was the reflective research design structured?
a: The research was conducted over one semester through three stages: preparation, implementation, and reflection. The final stage involved instructors engaging in a recorded discussion that was coded and analyzed to identify recurring themes.

q: What specific methods were used for the pre-learning phase?
a: Students watched five-minute instructional videos on discussion skills and completed connected tasks via a Learning Management System. These tasks included concept-checking pop quizzes and online forum discussions.

q: Who would benefit most from the application of this flipped learning approach?
a: The lesson video was particularly useful for students with lower proficiency in English, as they had the freedom to replay the video or slow it down if they needed to. Additionally, flipped learning offered learners a chance to control their learnings and helped students at different levels.

q: How did the shift to online learning affect instructor teaching methods?
a: Instructors were forced to adapt to different teaching approaches and implemented flipped learning by creating videos explaining target discussion skills and posting them in an online learning management system. They also adapted the EDC curriculum to fit an online learning context to accommodate the loss of time and face-to-face interaction.

q: What was the impact of the flipped learning model on instructor workload?
a: Instructors experienced a significant increase in workload due to the time-consuming preparation required to create high-quality, concise videos and assignments.

q: What types of pre-lesson tasks were used to assess student preparation?
a: Instructors developed pre-lesson tasks such as concept-checking pop quizzes and online forum discussions. These tasks helped instructors gain insights into specific student difficulties before class.

q: How can instructors use flipped learning to support differentiated instruction?
a: Instructors can use flipped learning to help students at different levels by providing lesson videos that lower-proficiency students can replay or slow down. For higher-proficiency students, assignments requiring language use, such as discussion board responses, ensure they are sufficiently challenged.

q: How does flipped learning change the use of in-class time?
a: Flipped learning utilizes class time for student-centered and interactive learning activities. This approach allows for maximized class time for student-centered activities and for achieving high-order skills such as analyzing, evaluating, and creating.

q: What logistical challenges were identified in the online teaching environment?
a: Instructors faced technical challenges as students adjusted to Zoom and dealt with unstable connections due to being in different locations. Additionally, much time was lost on organization and logistical matters, such as organizing students for online practice and discussions.

q: How was the Learning Management System (LMS) utilized in the online setting?
a: Instructors posted videos explaining target discussion skills in the LMS to implement flipped learning. Students used the system to watch these videos and complete connected tasks in preparation for classroom activities.

q: How did the instructors reflect on their implementation of the flipped learning model?
a: The instructors reflected on their experiences and observations after implementing flipped learning and pre-lesson tasks for one semester. They found that while it saved time, offered learners control over their learning, and helped students at different levels, challenges included time consumption and low motivation.

q: How are students categorized in the English Discussion Class (EDC) at Rikkyo University?
a: Students are sorted into four proficiency levels based on their Test of English for International Communication (TOEIC) scores. Level I represents the highest proficiency, while Level IV represents the lowest proficiency.

q: How does flipped learning facilitate differentiated instruction for students with varying English proficiency levels?
a: Lower proficiency students benefit from the ability to replay or slow down lesson videos and complete simpler assignments like gap-fills. Higher proficiency students are challenged through assignments that require language use, such as responding to peers on discussion boards.

q: What were the main findings regarding the specific types of student engagement observed?
a: Students exhibited fair to moderate levels of engagement regarding self-motivation and effort. However, engagement in interpersonal interactions, such as social chatting or getting to know peers, was notably low.

q: How did the researcher measure engagement and community among the students?
a: The researcher employed a quantitative approach using the Online Student Engagement (OSE) scale by Dixson (2015) and the Classroom Community Scale (CCS) by Rovai (2002). Data was collected via an anonymous Google Forms questionnaire.

q: What external factors were found to detrimentally affect student engagement?
a: The COVID-19 pandemic and natural calamities negatively impacted engagement due to mental and emotional stress. These external stressors also caused technical issues like power failures and poor internet connectivity.

q: What recommendations are made to universities to improve online student engagement?
a: To foster engagement, universities can encourage interaction through various communication and social media platforms. Additionally, official support from the university and the establishment of formal student organizations are suggested to help foster a sense of community.

q: Who would benefit most from the findings of this research?
a: Data suggests that official support from the university would be of benefit. Additionally, responses to the scales can serve as a basis for formulating approaches and strategies in learning design and teaching online classes at UPOU and other similar institutions.

q: How did students perceive their sense of community within their courses?
a: Students were largely neutral regarding their sense of community. While they felt encouraged to ask questions, they did not feel the course was "like a family" and reported a lack of interdependence.

q: What role does self-motivation play in the engagement levels of these students?
a: Students exhibited fair to moderate levels of engagement specifically regarding their self-motivation and effort. This suggests that while students are motivated to learn, they struggle with the social dimensions of engagement.

q: What are the four elements of a sense of community according to McMillan and Chavis (1986)?
a: The four elements are membership, which is a feeling of belonging, and influence, which is the belief in one's ability to make a difference. The remaining elements are reinforcement, involving the integration and fulfillment of needs, and a shared emotional connection.

q: What specific courses were selected for the BAMS program study?
a: The study involved two specific classes: MMS 100 (Introduction to Multimedia) and MMS 175 (Videography in Multimedia). MMS 100 is typically taken during a student's first year, while MMS 175 is usually taken during the third year or later.

q: What is the statistical correlation between student engagement and sense of community in the BAMS classes?
a: There is a moderate positive relationship between the two, indicated by a correlation coefficient of 0.422 at a statistical significance of α=.001. This result corroborates the link between student engagement and a sense of community.

q: What technical issues were identified as having a detrimental effect on student engagement?
a: Students reported that poor Internet connectivity and power failures acted as detrimental factors. These issues became more pronounced in certain areas due to the surge in nationwide use during home confinement.

q: What are the components of student engagement in traditional classrooms?
a: In traditional settings, engagement involves affective and behavioral components. These include skills, emotion, participation, and performance.

q: How did the BAMS students demonstrate motivation toward learning according to the CCS scale?
a: Students showed strong motivation, evidenced by a relatively strong disagreement with the statement that the course does not promote a desire to learn. Additionally, the OSE scale showed a high score for putting forth effort.

q: What are the limitations regarding the nature of the relationship between engagement and community in this research?
a: While correlation analysis establishes that a relationship exists, it cannot determine the specific nature of that relationship. It is unclear if engagement depends on community, if community depends on engagement, or if there is a synergy between them.

q: What role does teacher presence play in student behavior according to the research?
a: Teacher presence can impact how students behave even outside of the online classroom. While teachers are well-regarded as sources of encouragement, community building may require proactive involvement from students rather than just the instructor.

q: What were the primary findings regarding the support provided to students with disabilities?
a: The findings revealed that effective student support is the most important aspect of an ODeL institution. However, participants reported significant discrimination, a lack of prioritization of their needs, and feeling undervalued or neglected by institutions.

q: What research methodology was used to investigate these student experiences?
a: The researcher employed a qualitative approach within an interpretivism paradigm using an exploratory research design. Data was collected via MS Teams using purposive and snowball sampling to recruit 10 participants.

q: What specific accessibility hurdles did students with disabilities encounter?
a: Students with disabilities face physical barriers in higher education institutions and challenges accessing computer laboratories if facilities are not disability-friendly. They also encounter issues with the late delivery of study materials and technology for online examinations that is not disability-friendly.

q: What unique safety concerns were identified for students with albinism?
a: Students with albinism experience a high feeling of being unsafe and are being targeted and killed due to illogical myths. These myths include the mistaken belief that killing people with albinism for 'muthi' can make someone rich.

q: What specific academic support inequity was noted during the transition to online learning?
a: During the transition to online learning, the institution moved to online examinations without considering the need for students with disabilities to have extra time granted. Additionally, the technology used for online examinations was not disability-friendly.

q: What is the theoretical promise of ODeL for students with disabilities?
a: The ODeL strategy creates an enabling teaching and learning environment that leads to the full participation and equalization of opportunities for students with disabilities. This framework helps to create or open up learning opportunities that emphasize the social interaction of all students, including those with learning disabilities and certain physical disabilities.

q: How did the COVID-19 pandemic affect the foundation of ODeL delivery for students with disabilities?
a: The outbreak of Covid-19 compounded problems when the institution was compelled to move from a physical to an online examination without considering the need for SWDs to have extra time granted. Additionally, the technology used for online examinations was not disability-friendly, causing the challenges of SWDs to be ignored or not taken cognisance of.

q: What pressure are institutions of higher learning currently facing?
a: Institutions are under pressure to provide equal access to all students with diverse learning needs. They are also working to meet UN Sustainable Development Goals regarding the reduction of inequality.

q: How should institutions change their approach to being student-centered?
a: Institutions must include active consultation with students with disabilities during the design of policies and infrastructure. They should also integrate these voices into planning and budgeting processes.

q: What is identified as the most important aspect of an ODeL institution?
a: The most important aspect of an ODeL institution is effective student support. The research suggests that institutions are currently lagging in addressing the diverse needs of these students.

q: What safety concerns were specifically raised by students with albinism?
a: Students with albinism view safety as the most important aspect needing attention because they cannot walk freely in public due to living in fear for their lives. They also perceive that the university is not concerned about their mode of transport or how they get to campus, and that nobody is available to escort them to or from public transport.

q: How do the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals relate to the inclusion of students with disabilities in higher learning?
a: The inclusion of students with disabilities aligns with the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals to reduce inequality by 2030. This can be achieved by transforming institutions to ensure access to facilities, study materials, and necessary technology.

q: What specific accommodations are provided to students with disabilities in the USA?
a: Policies in the USA require higher education institutions to provide allowances to support academic needs. These may include extended exam time, the availability of a note-taker, or taking exams verbally instead of in writing.

q: What are the specific disability types represented in the research sample of ten participants?
a: The sample included two students with albinism, five with physical disabilities, and three who are visually impaired or challenged. The group consisted of seven females and three males.

q: What research method and design were used to evaluate the e-learning course?
a: The researchers used a survey research design involving an online evaluation questionnaire via Google Forms. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics such as frequency counts, percentages, median, and mode.

q: How did the researchers ensure the reliability of the evaluation instrument?
a: The researchers conducted a pretest with 15 students which yielded a Cronbach’s alpha value of 94.7516%. This indicates high internal consistency and reliability for the 24 favorable statements used in the tool.

q: What specific dimensions of Khan’s Eight-Dimensional E-Learning Framework were applied?
a: The study applied the Evaluation Dimension of the framework. This involved assessing learners, instruction, and the learning environment through six specific variables.

q: What specific areas of the e-learning experience require improvement according to the findings?
a: Interactivity is considered a bit low in the e-learning course. Students need to be encouraged to interact more with their classmates and provide feedback to their co-learners' ideas to facilitate fruitful discussions.

q: Who were the respondents involved in this evaluation?
a: The respondents were thirty-three international health learners enrolled in the IH 213 course during the second semester of Academic Year 2016-2017.

q: What were the specific variables used to assess the course?
a: The assessment focused on six variables: Relevance, Reflective Thinking, Tutor Support, Interactivity, Peer Support, and Interpretation.

q: Why is systematic evaluation important for ODeL programs?
a: Systematic evaluation provides a factual basis for making corrective adjustments. This is essential as learning environments become more open and complex.

q: What is the goal of applying evaluation frameworks to ODeL environments?
a: Applying these frameworks helps create more meaningful learning environments. It allows for the management and planning of increasingly complex open systems.

q: How can instructors improve interactivity within an e-learning course design?
a: The faculty-in-charge can add more graded discussion forums or incentives to encourage interactivity. Additionally, activities such as debates and group works that require students to respond to their classmates' ideas can be implemented.

q: What role does content relevance play in the IH 213 course design?
a: The course design was found to be effective because students reported the content was important to professional practice. The topics were also noted to be of interest to the learners.

q: What tool was used to ensure the reliability of the course evaluation?
a: The researchers used a pretest to calculate a Cronbach’s alpha value of 94.7516%. This confirmed the high reliability of the 24 statements adopted from the Moodle Self Assessment Tool.

q: What statistical methods were used to analyze the evaluation data?
a: Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. This included frequency counts, percentages, and measures of central tendency like median and mode.

q: How was the IH 213 e-learning course perceived by its students?
a: The course was perceived as highly effective in most dimensions. Students reported high levels of reflective thinking and effective tutor and peer support.

q: What was the main weakness identified in the IH 213 e-learning course?
a: The main weakness identified was that interactivity is a bit low in the e-learning course. This was shown by the fact that statements under Interactivity were mostly answered sometimes by the respondents.

q: Who participated in the evaluation of the IH 213 course?
a: The participants were thirty-three international health learners. They were enrolled in the Diploma in/Master of International Health Program at the University of the Philippines Open University.

q: What are the specific benefits of conducting an evaluation of an e-learning program?
a: Evaluation provides feedback that helps gain a better understanding of how a program or specific course is working. It also provides a factual basis for making decisions on operations and implementing corrective adjustments.

q: What research method and theoretical framework were used to analyze the student outputs?
a: The researchers employed a qualitative design using thematic analysis to examine 12 final sharing outputs, including integrative papers and videos. The analysis was guided by Kolb and Fry’s (1974) Experiential Learning Cycle as the theoretical framework.

q: How did students reflect on their experiences during the reflective observation stage?
a: Students reflected on challenges such as emotional struggles, managing multiple responsibilities, and minimal training in specific interventions. These reflections led to realizations regarding professional competencies, self-awareness, and the application of theory to practice.

q: What are the key conclusions regarding the effectiveness of online facilitation for field instruction?
a: The online nature of the FI courses and the online strategies used allowed for the facilitation of FI despite geographical limitations and changing learner needs. The open and distance e-learning framework maximized students' experiential learning through reflection and learning to help them become better practitioners.

q: What administrative improvements are suggested to facilitate the internship process?
a: Students recommended that the program require students to submit their proposed agency at least one semester before the course to complete requirements on time. Additionally, they suggested the institution establish partner agencies with long-term agreements to ensure available placements and prevent delays caused by searching for agencies and facilitating MOUs.

q: What were the limitations or challenges identified by the students during their field instruction?
a: The students identified emotional challenges such as fear, doubts, and hesitations, as well as challenges brought by multiple responsibilities. Practice-related challenges included minimal training in handling clients and cases and difficulty establishing better relationships with stakeholders.

q: How is 'experiential education' defined in the context of this research?
a: Experiential education refers to programs designed to widen learning experiences beyond the classroom and into work and community contexts. Internship programs are a specific type of experiential education used to develop practice skills and transition from theory to practice.

q: What specific challenges did students face during their field instruction experience?
a: Students encountered challenges categorized into emotional challenges, challenges brought by multiple responsibilities, and practice-related challenges. Emotional challenges included fears of becoming a social work administrator, being afraid to share observations, doubts about making it until 2020, and hesitations regarding taking Field Instruction I.

q: How is field instruction facilitated for geographically dispersed students in this program?
a: Field instruction is supervised and guided online by the faculty-in-charge via the MyPortal course site. This distance e-learning framework allows students to participate in internships despite being geographically dispersed.

q: What is the impact of the online mode of facilitation on student learning?
a: The online mode of facilitation enables students to maximize experiential learning and integrate theory and practice through guided reflection. This approach helps students become better practitioners and contributors to social transformation.

q: What theoretical framework was used to analyze the experiential learning process?
a: The study utilized Kolb and Fry’s (1974) Experiential Learning Cycle as a theoretical framework. This framework focuses on four stages: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation.

q: What are the requirements for students undergoing field instruction in the UPOU Social Work program?
a: Students are required to undergo 320 hours of supervised field instruction within reputable institutions. This instruction is supervised online by the faculty-in-charge through the MyPortal course site.

q: What are the three dimensions students use to frame their reflections during field instruction?
a: Students make reflections in reference to themselves as human beings, the profession as social workers, and their multiple responsibilities as online learners.

q: What are the primary benefits of participating in internship programs for students?
a: Internships provide course credits, work experience to help students become attractive to future employers, and a chance to test potential future careers. They also serve as a vital means to transition into the workplace for job placement.

q: How does experiential education differ from traditional learning focused on exams?
a: Experiential education enables students to learn to finish tasks as workers or community members rather than just students learning to pass exams. It emphasizes active participation in practical opportunities and the integration of study content into life.

q: What are the three specific relationships defined in experiential education?
a: The three relationships are the learner and the self, the learner and the teacher, and the learner and the learning environment. These relationships involve sense-making through reflection, interaction with a teacher who acts as a mediator, and engagement with the physical environment and people.

q: What is the central purpose of the research regarding collaborative learning in Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL)?
a: The research aims to identify themes constituting learners' views and experiences in collaborative learning activities within an R&D management online degree program. This helps to understand teaching and learning issues associated with adopting collaborative learning in ODeL environments.

q: What are the main findings regarding the purpose of collaborative learning for students?
a: Collaborative learning allows students to learn through interaction, information exchange, and experience sharing among group members. It provides an opportunity to learn from peers through the exchange of ideas and the social construction of knowledge by sharing diverse perspectives. Additionally, it helps learners deepen their understanding of lessons while expanding their views of concepts, issues, and situations.

q: What method was used to analyze the learner experiences in the Diploma in Research & Development Management program?
a: The researchers employed a meta-interpretive approach, which involves an interpretive synthesis of existing qualitative research. They used previous interpretations of learner views as raw data through an iterative coding process.

q: What are the primary challenges students face during online collaborative activities?
a: Challenges include difficulties in communicating through technology, negative attitudes of some learners on collaboration, and lack of individual accountability. Additionally, time and geographical differences, as well as the impact on course flexibility and the urgency to depend on co-learners for grades, pose challenges.

q: How is the teacher's role described in the context of online collaborative learning?
a: The teacher's role is a dual reality where their relative absence allows for informal student interaction, yet their active presence as a facilitator is highly valued. Students appreciate teachers who provide stimulating inputs, feedback, and a personal touch.

q: What are the key recommendations for designing and delivering online collaborative learning?
a: Teachers should provide clear instructions, clarify expectations, and offer online resources to enable exploration. It is also recommended to use peer review for co-creation of knowledge and accountability, while balancing structure with flexibility regarding resources, collaborators, and assessment methods.

q: What are the implications for the format of collaborative tasks in distance education?
a: Implementing collaborative learning in the ODeL environment requires a teacher to balance providing structure to lessen confusion with providing flexibility for exploration. Learners benefit from clear instructions, clarifying expectations, online resources, and peer review, while also appreciating flexibility regarding resources, group members, and assessment methods.

q: To whom are the findings of this research most applicable?
a: The findings can be applied to the two R&DM courses and also to similar courses and programs within and outside UPOU.

q: What specific obstacles impact the learner experience during online collaboration?
a: Specific obstacles include difficulties in communicating through technology, negative attitudes of some learners on collaboration, and lack of individual accountability. Additionally, challenges include time and geographical differences among learners, as well as limitations on flexibility and the urgency to depend on co-learners for grades.

q: What structural elements are recommended to support successful online collaborative learning?
a: Teachers need to provide enough structure to lessen confusion about the process of collaboration while providing enough flexibility to allow for exploration of ideas. Recommended elements include step-by-step guidelines, strategies for organizing meetings and assigning tasks, and guide questions to aid group discussions.

q: What is the recommended timing for implementing collaborative activities in a term?
a: One way to achieve this is to schedule the conduct of the learning activities in the early to middle part of the term when students are doing fewer course requirements. It was also not advisable to hold the activity at the latter part of the semester as around that time, the students would already be preparing for their final examinations.

q: How was a WebQuest utilized in the R&DM251 course?
a: The WebQuest was used as an inquiry-oriented activity involving internet resources and role-playing. It was designed to help students synthesize learning regarding technology evaluation mechanisms.

q: In which specific degree program was this research conducted?
a: The research was conducted within the Diploma in Research & Development Management (DR&DM) at the University of the Philippines Open University.

q: How does collaborative learning differ from cooperative learning?
a: Cooperative learning typically involves dividing a task among group members to construct one final product. In contrast, collaborative learning involves mutual discussion, active processing of information, analytical and critical thinking, and synthesis of the whole process.

q: What specific roles can students assume during the role-playing activity in the R&DM251 course?
a: Students may choose from the roles of technical director, scientist, engineer, and stakeholder. This role-playing approach allows students to answer questions through different perspectives.

q: What is the central problem addressed in Impact of Information Society Research in the Global South?
a: The book interrogates how research on ICTs in the Global South contributes to an information society through practical implementation, policy influence, and media coverage. It specifically seeks to identify concrete evidence regarding the impact of ICTs on socio-economic development objectives.

q: Why is there a push for 'homegrown' scholarship in this work?
a: The scholarship from the Global South presented in this book makes scrutiny of cases from the region to be more contextual and homegrown.

q: What barriers prevent researchers from influencing policy?
a: Barriers include the fact that most researchers do not go out of their way to promote their work. Additionally, many researchers do not communicate in a language other than that used in academia.

q: What are the broader implications for future ICT research?
a: The book opens doors towards uncharted research territories on the impacts of ICTs in development and offers directions for inquiry, particularly among novice researchers. It also brings to light several researchable areas through cases showing varying impacts of ICT initiatives.

q: How is the book structured to address its research questions?
a: The book is divided into two parts, with the first consisting of theoretical discussions on gauging ICT impacts and literature reviews on how ICT research can impact policies. The second part reports different cases of ICT applications and initiatives in various sectors, such as agriculture and education.

q: How does the book address the relationship between research and policy?
a: The book explores the intersections between research, practice, and policy by interrogating the impacts of ICTs in international development. It specifically examines how research on ICTs in the Global South plays a role in influencing policy formulation.

q: What factors hinder the quality of communication between researchers and policymakers?
a: Factors include that most researchers do not go out of their way to promote their work. Additionally, they often do not communicate in a language other than that used in academia.

q: What methodological approaches are recognized as relevant for ICTD research?
a: Participatory methods and approaches are recognized as being relevant throughout the book. Examples of such approaches include the work of May & Diga (2015) and Olivera, Ale, & Chib (2015).

q: How does the book emphasize the user perspective in ICTs?
a: The book highlights the user perspective by prioritizing the voices of primary stakeholders. This is achieved through a focus on strong contextual reference.

q: How could the readability of the second part of the book be improved?
a: Readability could be enhanced by adding more photos to establish the context of the ICTD case studies. This would help readers better imagine the described scenarios.

q: What suggestions are made regarding the presentation of tables and graphs?
a: Tables and graphs could be presented in a more engaging and visually appealing manner. Using infographics could help make the difficult content easier to digest.

q: What critique is offered regarding the content of part 2?
a: While part 2 is intended to focus on actual cases, some are based on literature reviews. It is suggested that more actual cases be added to reinforce the uniqueness of ICTD cases in the Global South.

q: How does the book's structure impact the reader's experience?
a: The first part of the book is heavy in theories and literature reviews. Consequently, the second part would benefit from more actual cases to balance the theoretical content.

q: Who is the intended audience for this book?
a: The book is described as an excellent resource for ICTD researchers. This includes both budding and established professionals.

q: What conversation has this book sparked within the field?
a: The book has sparked conversations regarding how to explore the impacts of ICTs in development. It encourages thinking about how to move research beyond academic confines.

q: What does the book provide reflections on regarding ICT research?
a: The book provides reflections on how to bring ICT research and relevance beyond the confines of academia. It aims to increase the impact of research in development contexts.

q: What role do photos play in understanding ICTD case studies?
a: Photos could establish the context of case studies. This would assist the reader in imagining the specific scenarios being described.

q: What is the central problem addressed in the assessment of graduate thesis practices at the Faculty of Management and Development Studies (FMDS)?
a: The study addresses the uncertainty regarding which administrative practices effectively promote quality thesis writing within an Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) context. It specifically looks at how spatial and temporal gaps between students and faculty complicate research supervision and administration.

q: What are the main findings regarding the current state of thesis practices in the FMDS programs?
a: Findings show that while programs implement many ideal practices like technology-based orientations and support systems, there are significant gaps between current practices and student needs. Students reported insufficient guidance, unclear quality expectations, and difficulties adhering to timelines.

q: What research methodology was used to investigate these thesis practices?
a: The researchers employed a qualitative approach involving content analysis of course guides and thesis manuals, interviews with Program Chairs and staff, and online surveys of current and former students. The study utilized the Triad of Quality Supervisory Practices and the Dynamic Facilitation framework as theoretical lenses.

q: Which specific Master's programs were included in this investigation?
a: The study examined four programs: Master of ASEAN Studies, Master of Arts in Nursing, Master of International Health, and Master of Land Valuation and Management.

q: What are the key recommendations for improving thesis administration in distance education?
a: Recommendations include explicitly defining high-quality thesis characteristics, providing advisers with training on online feedback technologies, and offering online research skill courses. The authors also suggest developing an automated learning management system for advising and promoting learner-learner interaction.

q: How does the 'distance-ness' of the programs affect the student experience?
a: In the context of ODeL, problems can be magnified because distance learners are more diverse and there is time and geographical difference between students and their advisers. Due to these differences, distance learners writing their thesis tend to experience more stress.

q: Who are the primary stakeholders affected by these thesis administration practices?
a: The practices involve and impact graduate students, faculty members, advisers, program chairs, and administrative staff. The findings are particularly relevant to those managing thesis courses in an ODeL environment.

q: What are the implications of developing an automated learning management system for thesis advising?
a: An automated system for monitoring research work progress can enable both teachers and learners to be notified of their deliverables and deadlines. Additionally, a learning management system suited for thesis advising in the online mode must be developed to improve the monitoring of students’ progress and to better facilitate the interactions between students and their advisers.

q: How must thesis practices at UPOU align with the institution's educational model?
a: Because UPOU is an Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) institution, thesis practices implemented by Faculty Offices must adhere to the principles of distance education. This requires addressing the unique spatial and temporal gaps between students and faculty.

q: What theoretical frameworks were used to establish quality criteria in this ODeL context?
a: The study utilized the Triad of Quality Supervisory Practices by Chrispen et al. (2012) and the Dynamic Facilitation framework by Quan-Baffour and Vambe (2008). These frameworks helped establish criteria for quality in the distance mode.

q: What support systems are currently in place for students in the FMDS programs?
a: Current support systems include library services and monitoring task forces. Programs also use technology for orientations through video conferencing and web streaming.

q: What specific challenges do students face regarding guidance and feedback?
a: Students reported experiencing insufficient advice from teachers and unclear expectations regarding what constitutes a quality master’s thesis. They also faced difficulties in setting up meetings with members of the advising committee.

q: What are some examples of ideal practices currently implemented by the FMDS programs?
a: The four programs currently implement a set of prerequisites for enrolment to the graduate thesis course, a prescribed period for thesis completion, and various means for orientation to the thesis course. They also utilize criteria for adviser selection and evaluation of thesis course related outputs, progress monitoring mechanisms, various modes for adviser and advisee communication, available student support services, activities and venues for student interaction, and means to encourage knowledge sharing and utilization.

q: What are the suggested best practices for improving thesis quality in ODeL?
a: It is suggested that programs focus on clarifying what constitutes a quality thesis in their disciplines, equipping advisers to maximize online technologies for communicating complex ideas, and scheduling deliverables. Additionally, programs should promote learner-learner interactions and provide open online courses on research skills to better prepare students. A learning management system suited for online thesis advising should also be developed to improve progress monitoring and facilitate student-adviser interactions.

q: What administrative challenges arise from the distance-learning format?
a: In the context of ODeL, problems can be magnified because distance learners are more diverse and there is time and geographical difference between students and their advisers. Additionally, setting up consultation meetings can be challenging due to the spatial and temporal distance between thesis students and advisers.

q: How can technology improve the administration of graduate theses?
a: An automated learning management system could improve administration by providing manuscript repositories and automated notifications for deadlines. This would help in better monitoring research progress.

q: How can the preparation for a thesis course be improved for distance learners?
a: The authors suggest offering open online courses on fundamental research skills, such as technical writing and statistical methods. This would better prepare students before they begin their actual thesis work.

q: What role does interaction play in the success of a thesis course in an ODeL setting?
a: Promoting learner-learner interaction among thesis students in the course site can help them learn from each other through the exchange of ideas and experiences in research and thesis writing. Additionally, a learning management system suited for thesis advising in the online mode could be developed to better facilitate interactions between students and their advisers.

q: What is the central problem investigated by Vilela-Malabanan and Echavez?
a: The research investigates the specific constraints encountered by academics when using a learning management system within a blended learning environment. The study seeks to understand why the uptake of these systems is not maximized by students and academics despite the reported benefits of educational technologies.

q: What research methodology was employed to conduct this investigation?
a: The researchers used a mixed-methods design involving qualitative in-depth interviews with thirty-three academics and a quantitative descriptive statistical analysis of Moodle computer logs. The qualitative data were analyzed using a grounded theory approach, while the quantitative data were processed using a simple data mining procedure.

q: How does the nature of a subject matter influence the constraints faced by academics?
a: Curriculum level constraints are related to whether a course is technology-driven or non-technology driven. Technology-driven courses, such as Engineering or Computer Science, require computer facilities or practical laboratory components, whereas non-technology driven courses like Arts & Social Sciences often do not require computer laboratories.

q: What role does student economic status play in the use of the learning management system?
a: Low usage of interactive features was strongly influenced by students’ economic viability and access. Additionally, students' access and economic viability were found to be constraints that caused difficulties for academics in delivering courses in a technology-enhanced learning environment.

q: What specific time management difficulties do academics report?
a: Academics reported time management constraints related to the preparation of learning materials and tests, course implementation, contact hours, compensation, and time wasted due to connectivity problems. Additionally, the amount of time required to attend training, prepare materials, and interact or manage discussions online was noted as a context of time management.

q: What are the concerns regarding academic integrity in a blended learning environment?
a: The major issues regarding academic integrity involve the element of trust when assessment tasks are performed outside the classroom, specifically regarding the validity and veracity of students' answers. Concerns were particularly related to scheduled online tests and assignments, as instructors could not personally supervise students taking tests in internet cafés, residences, or open laboratories.

q: What is the scope and setting of this research?
a: The study was conducted at a state university in Mindanao, Philippines, involving thirty-three academics from various disciplines and professorial levels. The specific system analyzed was Moodle, customized as the MSU-IIT Online Learning Environment (MOLE).

q: How does preparing digital materials affect the workload of academics?
a: Material preparation for blended learning was found to be more time consuming as compared to that of the traditional classroom. Participants revealed that writing lesson notes, looking for relevant links, and assessment of learning outcomes were time consuming tasks.

q: What academic anxieties are reported regarding online assessments?
a: Academics experience anxiety regarding the validity of control and the veracity of student answers during unsupervised online quizzes. They worry about whether students are performing tasks themselves when working outside the classroom.

q: How does the subject matter affect the effectiveness of the blended learning environment?
a: Descriptive subjects are better delivered online compared to problem-solving or computational subjects. Highly computational and technical subjects, such as Engineering courses, often have computer or practical laboratory components that require specific facilities to use intended teaching strategies.

q: What characterizes the socio-technological landscape of the studied learning environment?
a: The environment is a blended learning setting characterized by a mix of traditional face-to-face and web-based technologies. It involves the use of the Moodle learning management system, though usage is influenced by personal and environmental issues.

q: What are the four major dimensions of constraints identified by the researchers?
a: The four dimensions are time management, curriculum level, students' access and economic viability, and students' work and validity of control. These factors prevent the full maximization of the LMS.

q: How do economic factors act as a constraint for students?
a: Economic reasons cause many students to lack their own computers or an internet connection at home. These economic challenges and issues with economic viability contribute to low usage of interactive features in the system logs.

q: What specific LMS platform is utilized at MSU-IIT?
a: The university uses the Moodle platform for its learning environment. This platform is customized and referred to as the MSU-IIT Online Learning Environment (MOLE).

q: Which specific LMS activities are classified as interactive?
a: Interactive activities include quizzes, forums, blogs, chats, and journal activities. Among these, the forum was the most frequently used by academics, while the quiz generated the highest total number of interactions.

q: What factors determine the adoption and diffusion of LMSs by academic staff according to Macharia and Nyakwende?
a: The characteristics of Vice Chancellors or CEOs, such as visionary ICT leadership and keenness on modern ICTs, are important determinants. Additionally, organizational variables like top management support, availability of ICTs, and organizational readiness relate to the behavioral intentions of staff.

q: What are the main findings regarding the impact of computer-based simulation on student knowledge?
a: Computer-based simulations effectively increased knowledge across all three learning groups. The advanced group showed the greatest increase in mean scores, followed by the proficient and approaching proficiency groups.

q: What was the research method and design used to investigate these effects?
a: The researchers used a quasi-experimental research design involving 143 students from three intact classes. Data were collected through pre-tests, post-tests, an interest survey, and focus group discussions.

q: How did computer-based simulations affect student interest in Chemistry?
a: Advanced and proficient students reported high interest in learning through simulation, while students approaching proficiency reported moderate interest. Qualitative data showed students enjoyed the gamified elements and the ability to work independently.

q: What are the key conclusions regarding the role of simulations in the classroom?
a: Computer-based simulation is recommended to be employed in classroom instruction to increase students' knowledge and interest in Chemistry. Students suggested that these activities should be used as a reinforcement activity to avoid waste of time and to help students be aware of the topic's background.

q: What are the limitations or specific conditions suggested for using simulations effectively?
a: Computer-based simulation should be used most especially in topics that are hard to visualize and unsafe to perform in the laboratory. Additionally, the design of learning activities should be given a higher level of priority than the use of instructional technology when employing computer simulations in the classroom.

q: What are the implications for future research in this field?
a: Further research must investigate the effects when students fully or do not fully engage in computer-assisted activities. Additionally, considerable continuing research is needed to identify and resolve issues that arise when individual differences are considered.

q: What features of the technology contributed to student enjoyment?
a: Students enjoyed the simulation because of the stars they virtually receive and the challenging game levels. They also appreciated that the material is easy to manipulate, allows for minimal supervision to foster independence, and includes practice exercises and games after topic introductions.

q: What methods were used to assess student knowledge and interest?
a: Knowledge was measured using pre-tests and post-tests. Interest was measured using an interest survey adapted from the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory.

q: How do computer-based simulations assist with difficult Chemistry topics?
a: Computer-based simulation is useful in understanding the movements of atoms and molecules and helps students understand concepts in a simpler and faster way. It is particularly useful for visualizing Chemistry concepts and topics that are hard to visualize or unsafe to perform in the laboratory.

q: What qualitative benefits did students report when using computer-based simulations?
a: Students reported that computer-based simulations are very useful in understanding the movements of atoms and molecules, helping them understand concepts in a simpler and faster way through real-time visualization. They also found the activities enjoyable and challenging due to graphics, stars, and game levels, which helped them learn concepts independently.

q: How did the use of simulations impact the knowledge levels of the different student groups?
a: Computer-based simulations effectively increased knowledge across all three learning groups. The advanced group showed the greatest increase in mean scores, followed by the proficient and approaching proficiency groups.

q: What specific type of knowledge is difficult for students to master in Chemistry?
a: Students struggle to develop fluency across symbolic, macroscopic, and particulate representations. This difficulty is a central challenge in mastering Chemistry.

q: How did interest levels vary among the different student proficiency groups?
a: Advanced and proficient students reported high interest in learning through simulation. In contrast, students approaching proficiency reported only moderate interest.

q: What gamified elements were found to increase student interest?
a: Students were interested because of the virtual stars they received and the challenges posed by game levels. These elements contributed to the enjoyment of the learning process.

q: What are the specific reasons students reported enjoying the use of computer-based simulations in Chemistry?
a: Students enjoyed the simulations because they were easy to manipulate and allowed for independent work with minimal supervision. They also appreciated the challenging game levels, the virtual stars received, and the ability to choose between topic introductions, practice, or games.

q: What was the primary purpose of the Digital Collective project at the University of the Philippines Open University?
a: The project aimed to engage students and alumni to co-create multimedia learning materials like graphics, audio, and blogs. It sought to move beyond faculty-centric models of Open Educational Resources (OERs) and support open educational practice.

q: What were the main findings regarding student participation in the Digital Collective?
a: While there were over fifty Facebook Group members, the majority were 'passive' participants who would almost never contribute to discussions or ask questions. Only a handful could be considered active participants, and even fewer would commit to creating content.

q: What research method was used to investigate the successes and failures of the project?
a: The investigation involved self-reflection, review of project notes, and a group discussion with some participants. The group discussion was conducted to gather data from the most active among nearly 60 participants.

q: What cultural factor was identified as a barrier to student contribution?
a: The cultural factor identified is "hiya," a Filipino term that translates to shame and can be rooted in a fear of disgrace or embarrassment. It may result in participants lacking the confidence to share their work publicly alongside peers.

q: Who would benefit most from the findings of this research?
a: The preliminary findings can hopefully help the university in drawing up a plan that can effectively build this online community.

q: What structural limitations hindered the project's ability to compete with students' other responsibilities?
a: The project was unable to secure incorporation in the curriculum, meaning work on the project was at or near the bottom of the participants' lists. Additionally, the head of the group did not set up any clear organization or hierarchy among members, which increased the challenge for active participants to collaborate with passive ones.

q: What specific types of multimedia materials were students and alumni encouraged to co-create?
a: Participants were encouraged to create various multimedia learning materials, including graphics, audio content, blogs, and stock photography.

q: Why did many participants in the Digital Collective remain passive despite successful recruitment?
a: Participants had other commitments such as work, family, and health that often took precedence. Additionally, participation in the project was not a top priority, especially since it lacked integration with formal coursework.

q: How does the concept of 'hiya' impact the student experience in co-creation projects?
a: It is possible that hiya caused participants to lack the confidence to put their work out in public alongside their peers. Additionally, students may have harbored fear or shame regarding the prospect of personally disappointing the facilitator.

q: How does the Digital Collective project relate to Open Educational Resources (OERs)?
